text:
𝐀 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐭𝐨𝐫: 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲’𝐬 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐇𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲

Prince Harry, the lad who once charmed a nation, has managed quite the transformation: from beloved royal to poster boy for betrayal. In centuries past, he’d be dragged to the Tower with little ceremony, his name whispered with distaste over tankards of ale. Today, he basks in California sunshine, preaching authenticity while ghosting the very traditions that made him. Truly, a modern traitor for modern times.

For what else could we call a prince who has traded his duty for Netflix deals, swapped family loyalty for public therapy sessions, and thrown his heritage to the wind in favour of a victim narrative? Picture it: Harry, once a soldier in Afghanistan, now waging a different sort of war—a tireless battle against his own past, as he sits in his Montecito mansion. Gone are the days of duty and decorum; now it’s all about the next “revelation,” the next family gripe aired to anyone still willing to listen.

Of course, there’s Meghan, sharing in this saga as if they’re star-crossed lovers in a production of 𝘙𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘰 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘑𝘶𝘭𝘪𝘦𝘵: 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘎𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘷𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘠𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘴. Together, they’ve built an empire on carefully curated angst, dressing up their defection as a noble quest for “freedom.” And yet, one can’t help but wonder if Harry’s “freedom” really amounts to little more than a gilded cage of their own making.

Meanwhile, back in Britain, Prince William quietly shoulders the legacy Harry discarded, preparing himself for kingship. His royal path is steady, measured—a role fulfilled with grace. Harry, on the other hand, seems more determined to stamp his name as a rogue prince, thumbing his nose at history as he clings to the fleeting rewards of his rebellion.

If Harry hoped to cement himself as some romantic figure, a maverick hero for the ages, he’s sorely mistaken. Instead, he’s  joined a long list of deserters and disgraced figures, his place in history etched not with respect but with regret. Because at the end of the day, there’s little noble in betrayal, no honour in disloyalty, and no lasting glory in the desertion of one’s own family. For a modern prince, he’s carved out a legacy steeped in treachery—one that history will neither forget nor forgive.

AND WHERE HARRY GOES,    ME  GAIN  CANNOT BE FAR BEHIND.

text:
𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐡𝐚𝐧: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐚𝐛𝐞 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥𝐬
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, have found themselves in a peculiar position, attempting to fashion a life of American royalty. It’s a laughable endeavour, particularly for a couple that fled to America under the pretense of seeking freedom from royal duty—only to realise they were rejected by the very Hollywood they sought to embrace.

𝐀 𝐑𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥 𝐅𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐞

Let’s cut to the chase: America has no use for royalty. The nation was forged in the spirit of independence and self-reliance, yet Harry and Meghan seem to have missed the memo. They have attempted to declare themselves as America’s answer to the royal family, but this self-proclaimed status is as welcome as a bull in a china shop.

After stepping back from royal duties, they made a beeline for Los Angeles, ready to conquer the American entertainment industry. To their dismay, Hollywood did not roll out the red carpet. Instead, they found themselves sidelined, their initial allure fading faster than Meghan’s acting career. The allure of royal heritage doesn’t hold much weight in America.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐈𝐥𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐮𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞

What’s particularly galling about their pursuit of status is the sheer hypocrisy that drips from every move they make. They preach about the importance of mental health and social justice, yet they reside in a mansion that screams privilege. Their glossy brand of activism is reminiscent of a Hollywood film script—polished but lacking genuine connection.

Their foundation, Archewell, is presented as a beacon of hope, yet it feels more like a vehicle for self-aggrandisement than true philanthropy. Their lives have become a never-ending PR campaign, hoping to cultivate an image that resonates with the public. But here’s the kicker: it’s transparent, and people see through it.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐑𝐞𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

Harry and Meghan’s delusion of grandeur only deepens as they navigate this new world. They may fancy themselves as the new American royalty, but the truth is that their grandiose ambitions have been met with indifference. The public isn’t clamouring for their opinions or seeking their endorsement on social issues. Instead, they are the subjects of mockery, the unwelcome guests at a party they weren’t invited to.

In a country that embraces individualism, their attempts to establish themselves as a royal couple are met with laughter. Their attempts to assert themselves as important figures are a stark reminder that the American people have no need for a modern-day fairy tale featuring a couple so out of touch.

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐛𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐀𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

In the end, Harry and Meghan’s aspirations to claim a space in American society as royalty are not only misguided—they are patently absurd. Their royal titles may remain, but in America, titles mean nothing. The essence of royalty is tied to duty, service, and, dare we say, sacrifice—all of which they seem to have cast aside in favour of self-promotion.

As they navigate their manufactured identities, it becomes painfully clear that the couple is merely grasping at straws. Let them parade their aspirations, but let it be known: America has enough self-made royalty to contend with. They don’t need another pair of out-of-touch aristocrats attempting to rewrite the narrative.

author: @ocdman202
text:
𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐡𝐚𝐧: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐚𝐧𝐧𝐚𝐛𝐞 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥𝐬 GRIFTING FROM NETFLIX NOW.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, have found themselves in a peculiar position, attempting to fashion a life of American royalty. It’s a laughable endeavour, particularly for a couple that fled to America under the pretense of seeking freedom from royal duty—only to realise they were rejected by the very Hollywood they sought to embrace.

𝐀 𝐑𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥 𝐅𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐞

Let’s cut to the chase: America has no use for royalty. The nation was forged in the spirit of independence and self-reliance, yet Harry and Meghan seem to have missed the memo. They have attempted to declare themselves as America’s answer to the royal family, but this self-proclaimed status is as welcome as a bull in a china shop.

After stepping back from royal duties, they made a beeline for Los Angeles, ready to conquer the American entertainment industry. To their dismay, Hollywood did not roll out the red carpet. Instead, they found themselves sidelined, their initial allure fading faster than Meghan’s acting career. The allure of royal heritage doesn’t hold much weight in America.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐈𝐥𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐥𝐮𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞

What’s particularly galling about their pursuit of status is the sheer hypocrisy that drips from every move they make. They preach about the importance of mental health and social justice, yet they reside in a mansion that screams privilege. Their glossy brand of activism is reminiscent of a Hollywood film script—polished but lacking genuine connection.

Their foundation, Archewell, is presented as a beacon of hope, yet it feels more like a vehicle for self-aggrandisement than true philanthropy. Their lives have become a never-ending PR campaign, hoping to cultivate an image that resonates with the public. But here’s the kicker: it’s transparent, and people see through it.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐑𝐞𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

Harry and Meghan’s delusion of grandeur only deepens as they navigate this new world. They may fancy themselves as the new American royalty, but the truth is that their grandiose ambitions have been met with indifference. The public isn’t clamouring for their opinions or seeking their endorsement on social issues. Instead, they are the subjects of mockery, the unwelcome guests at a party they weren’t invited to.

In a country that embraces individualism, their attempts to establish themselves as a royal couple are met with laughter. Their attempts to assert themselves as important figures are a stark reminder that the American people have no need for a modern-day fairy tale featuring a couple so out of touch.

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐛𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐀𝐬𝐩𝐢𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

In the end, Harry and Meghan’s aspirations to claim a space in American society as royalty are not only misguided—they are patently absurd. Their royal titles may remain, but in America, titles mean nothing. The essence of royalty is tied to duty, service, and, dare we say, sacrifice—all of which they seem to have cast aside in favour of self-promotion.

As they navigate their manufactured identities, it becomes painfully clear that the couple is merely grasping at straws. Let them parade their aspirations, but let it be known: America has enough self-made royalty to contend with. They don’t need another pair of out-of-touch aristocrats attempting to rewrite the narrative.

Imagine you’re about to host friends for dinner. How would you go about it?

It’s simple. You start in the lush, verdant garden that abuts some random estate, strolling through rows of ripe, juicy berries, gathering tomatoes, squash blossoms and jewel-toned lettuce leaves in a dainty wicker basket. Then you stop by an apiary and collect fresh honey.

I don’t even know why I’m telling you this, it’s so obvious. Also, your husband is a prince.  (known as Hazben)

If this wasn’t all immediately evident to you – wow, embarrassing! But – don’t worry. This week, the trailer dropped for Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex’s new Netflix show, With Love, Meghan, which premieres on 15 January. According to Netflix, the series, produced by the duchess, “reimagines the genre of lifestyle programming” by “blending practical how-to’s and candid conversations with friends, new and old”.

“We’re not in the pursuit of perfection,” Meghan assures us from somewhere deep inside a Nancy Meyers-esque farmhouse kitchen the size of a small airplane hangar. “We’re in the pursuit of joy!” According to Elle Decor, the Thermador stove and range seen in the trailer could set one back anywhere from $12,000 to $16,000.

The trailer, which looks like a “quiet luxury” Pinterest board come to life, is a symphony of beige: beige sweaters, beige hummus, beige focaccia, personalized beige candles and an assortment of beige flowers. “I see what color I gravitate to, and everything goes from there,” Meghan says, re: beige flower arrangements.

author: @bramsrockhopper3377
text:
Good grief. The fakery is unreal. 🤦🏻‍♀️ 

That house isn’t hers, nor that beautiful garden. We know that, because we were told they were filming in a different location. Why? Straight away it’s inauthentic (to borrow her favourite claim). It’s just a set. So to use it as the base for this whole “look I’m so natural and free and authentic and wholesome and these are my bestest friends and haven’t I created an amazing life!” thing is utterly, tangibly, false. So she requires a whole different location, set designers, make up artist, hair stylist, other stylists no doubt, and probably a whole gang of people actually creating this food in the background, in order to try to make herself look good? She can’t just cook in her own mansion with her own things around her? Wow. Okaaay.

I predict another own goal. The woman whose name is actually a saying for ghosting friends (to be Markled) and who has famously said awful and untrue things about her family and her husband’s family is now going to preach to us about friendship and togetherness and being kind and generous? Wow. Do me a lemon 🍋 

This is such a blatant attempt at a rebrand. Again. 🥱 

Just my opinions. I was happy for a Harry at the start, celebrated their wedding, wished them the best, but the more I’ve seen the more I’ve just run in the opposite direction. Proved themselves to be an awful pair. Untrustworthy, manipulative, false, mean and bitter, and always…always…the victimhood. Attacking everyone on one side, and claiming to be the victims on the other. So exhausting.
Again, just my opinions.

Netflix, you utter muppets. Just stop already. You’ve damaged your reputation quite enough through these two. What tawdry offerings for all that money… Like Polo, this is neither the time nor the way to appeal to people struggling with just trying to keep going in these difficult times. This “look how rich I am - but you can do it too!” bs is so inappropriate right now.

Imho

text:
Stepping Down From The Crown Is Proving To Be Quite Lucrative For Prince Harry And Meghan Markle
By: Emma Freire
September 16, 2021         ( another older article you might enjoy)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the former duke and duchess of Sussex, have taken America by storm. Their arrival on our shores is reminiscent of the British invasion in the 1960s. Except, instead of selling music, Harry and Meghan are here to sell us their ideas and personas. They haven’t just quit working for the royal family, they found a better gig.


Their post-royal trajectory resembles that of post-presidency Barack and Michelle Obama. Harry and Meghan give interviews, publish books, and launch charitable ventures. This is earning them a fortune, but they still claim to be victims.

The couple left the British royal family, a move dubbed “Megxit” in the press, in January 2020. Since then, they have rarely been off the front pages. Harry made headlines when he blamed “mass-scale misinformation” for COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy during a virtual appearance at the GQ Men of the Year awards on September 2.

Harry and Meghan embrace every standard liberal position, particularly a horror of people getting information from any source other than legacy media outlets and institutions.

In March, Prince Harry joined the Aspen Institute’s new Commission on Information Disorder. The commission’s stated aim is to “wrestle with the impact and problem of mis- and disinformation across all aspects of modern society, from the 2020 election and vaccine safety…” They hope to “engage disaffected populations who have lost faith in evidence-based reality.”

If you object to a British prince telling American citizens what they should believe about their own presidential election, then you are out of touch. Harry and his fellow commission members, who include Katie Couric, Garry Kasparov, and Kathryn Murdoch (daughter-in-law of Rupert), inhabit a rarefied circle that transcends old-fashioned notions like nationality.

When Harry and Meghan announced Megxit, they said they wanted to “work to become financially independent.” They have achieved that goal and then some. Like the Obamas, they have a Netflix deal estimated to be worth over $100 million. Like the Obamas, they have a podcast deal with Spotify estimated to be worth $25 million. To date, however, the only memorable moment of their podcast was their toddler Archie joining them to say “happy new year.”

Like the Obamas, they also have a book deal. They were paid around $20 million to write four books, including Harry’s memoir. Meghan had already published a children’s book called “The Bench” whose aim she says is “to depict another side of masculinity — one grounded in connection, emotion, and softness.”

Like the Obamas, Harry and Meghan have launched a charitable foundation. It’s called Archewell. According to its website, Archewell’s mission is to “unleash the power of compassion to drive systemic cultural change.”

Meghan celebrated her 40th birthday with an initiative called 40×40 in which she asked 40 friends to spend 40 minutes mentoring a woman who lost her job in the pandemic back into the workforce. Some of the people who have signed up for 40×40, like Sheryl Sandberg, make sense. Others, like Amanda Gorman, are less obvious. It’s hard to imagine what kind of career advice the 23-year-old who is best-known for reading a poem at Joe Biden’s inauguration could offer.

No one would be paying Harry and Meghan so much attention and money were it not for their connection to the British royal family. Despite being members of the institution that for the past 1,000 years was the very definition of privilege, Harry and Meghan like to present themselves as victims. They were chased out of their palace in the UK, and they sought refuge in a $14 million mansion in California.

In interviews, Harry regularly draws parallels between Meghan and his mother, Diana, the beloved and tragic princess who died in 1997. He told Oprah, “History was repeating itself. My mother was chased to her death while she was in a relationship with someone that wasn’t white and now look what’s happened.” If there is any truth to that, it is only in the sense of Marx’s famous words that history repeats itself, first as tragedy then as farce.

Is it any wonder Harry and Meghan prefer their new life in California over the slog and restrictions of royal duty? They can rake in millions; they can say and do whatever they please with no one holding them to account; and, at the end of the day, they can still claim to be victims.

Back in Britain, the royal family has weathered Megxit fairly well. By now, Harry and Meghan have given so many interviews bashing the royals that the novelty has worn off and most members of the British public are fed up with them. Harry suffered a huge drop in his approval rating in Britain. In fact, he has crashed even further than his father Prince Charles did in the 1990s after his divorce from Princess Diana.

Do Harry and Meghan care? Probably not. The British public isn’t their target audience anymore. They have transcended royalty. As long as Netflix and Spotify continue to pay, they will carry on as they are.

text:
There are plenty of reasons to hate Meghan Markle, so why did she just give us a whole Netflix season of more ammo? From stabbing the royal family in the back after having her entire life subsidized by British taxpayers to earning $25 million from Spotify for a few middling podcast episodes, Markle is a villainous figure who rakes in hate, not the praise and fandom she is clearly desperate for.

When Markle made her grand return to Instagram this New Year after dramatically quitting social media in 2021, it wasn’t for funsies. It was to announce and promote her new eight-part Netflix show, “With Love, Meghan.” 
From the teaser trailer she shared, the series appears to be Markle’s best attempt at LARPing Martha Stewart with her celebrity pals on her $15 million Montecito compound. “I’m going to share some tips and tricks,” Markle says as she peruses the flower market and sprinkles dried flowers on top of glazed donuts.

“We’re not in the pursuit of perfection. We’re in the pursuit of joy!” she exclaims with an acute degree of inauthenticity. The copy is dripping with feigned platitudes and the images are suspiciously rife with royal ripoffs. This trailer is so cringe-inducing that it physically makes my eyes twitch.

What’s most surprising about this product is that there was no one close enough to her to wave their hands and gently guide her in the complete opposite direction. When Netflix came knocking, what pitches did she turn down when she opted for this Ballerina Farm wannabe vanity project? Did no one who loves her suggest a series with a bit more sympathetic angle? A reality show where she helps down-and-out folks find a new home? A docu-series where she visits small, but beautiful American cities, highlighting everyday heroes?

I’m just shooting from the hip, and these may not be streaming hits, but the fact that no one close to her advised her against her casual yet glamourous homemaker shtick (or they did and she didn’t listen) says a lot about the type of person she surrounds herself with. Ironically, that’s also what we mainly learn from the teaser trailer guest list — that Markle spends her time arranging flowers and beekeeping with some of the most affluent and out-of-touch celebrities in her Hollywood bubble. “This is probably one of the most glamourous moments of my life,” gushes Mindy Kaling.

And it’s important to clarify here that the snobbery does not come from the idea of picture-perfect homemaking. This type of nearly unattainable farm-to-table perfection is what skyrocketed and sustained Martha Stewart, Ina Garten, Ballerina Farm, and waves of Instagram influencers following in their footsteps. Women do not loathe these women for their ideas or talents. We gobble them up and strive to emulate their recipes and cabinet paint colors in our own kitchens. No, it’s the laughable idea that the privileged princess, the Hollywood actress-turned-diva-sister-in-law, and royal golddigger who excommunicated her husband from his family, is someone we trust as a source for bringing joy and life into our own homes.

The only plausible explanation for Markle’s vanity project is that she relishes victimhood so much that she doesn’t care what the haters say because their critiques and comments sustain her signature victim mentality. Knowing she will never be the beloved people’s princess like her late mother-in-law, she’s stopped trying and settled for the loathed queen of Montecito.  She is just someone who invites the dislikes.

text:
I have never used AI before but was curious how it would write a review for this show.

A Review of the Netflix Cooking Show Starring Meghan Markle

Alas, dear readers, permit me to recount an experience most grievous, one that verily tested the very limits of my patience and faculties. It was a curious and lamentable occasion when I, in the misguided hope of finding some humble entertainment, ventured into the world of Netflix's culinary spectacle, with none other than the Duchess of Sussex, that selfsame Meghan Markle, as its star.

From the outset, I was struck by a sense of profound bewilderment—nay, despondency—at the spectacle presented before me. The show, intended to be a celebration of gastronomic delight, was rather an insipid parade of ostentation. Each dish, prepared with a certain air of indifference, seemed bereft of any true soul, as though the very joy of cooking had been trampled underfoot by the heavy hand of celebrity.

Miss Markle, whose voice carried a sweetness befitting of a spring morning, nevertheless fell short of conveying the warmth and simplicity one might expect from a true culinary enthusiast. Instead, one is left with the impression of a lady playing at being a cook, rather than a woman who has mastered the art in earnest. Her culinary ‘wisdom,’ such as it was, lacked depth and veracity. The steps were hardly instructive and the ingredients, more often than not, seemed like mere props in a stage performance, rather than essential components of a true dish.

It is no exaggeration to say that the entire production reeked of an affectation too conspicuous for its own good. The set, so lavish and gleaming, could hardly conceal the hollowness of the undertaking. In the place of charm or humility, there was a palpable air of self-importance, as though we were being led through a royal kitchen tour, not by a chef, but by one who had little more to offer than her own celebrity.

Oh, how I yearned for a simpler time, when cooking was done with heart, not with the camera in mind, and when food was shared for the sake of nourishment, not to pander to the fickle whims of an audience. In the end, the show left me with naught but a sense of melancholy, as though I had tasted a dish that promised much but delivered little.

In conclusion, dear reader, if you seek true culinary insight, I implore you to look elsewhere. For this, I daresay, is a show not for the true connoisseur, but for those who seek the glimmer of celebrity rather than the substance of a meal. Thus, I leave you with a heavy heart and an even heavier stomach—unfulfilled, and bereft of the warmth that true cooking so graciously bestows.

text:
𝐈𝐬 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐥𝐞? 

That’s the question on everyone’s lips as the Duke of Sussex slowly, and somewhat tragically, comes to grips with the storm he’s waded into. For years, the world watched with morbid curiosity as Prince Harry fell under the spell of the cable actress who seemed to promise him the kind of liberation he thought he craved. But now, it appears the fog might be lifting.

Ever since he and Meghan Markle packed up their royal obligations and moved stateside, Harry has been like a lost puppy. Yes, he’s had the bright lights of Montecito and the comforting hum of Netflix millions to keep him warm, but let’s not pretend that anything about their lives has been a fairy tale. He’s gone from being one of the most loved members of the royal family to a footnote on the latest podcast ranking. Once a cheeky, beloved prince, he now seems diminished, frequently wielding accusations against his own flesh and blood, all in the name of “truth-telling” while sporting a perpetual look of someone who's swallowed a bee.

Of course, Meghan clings to the spotlight with the fervour of someone whose star is slowly dimming. The glossy sheen she’s worked so hard to maintain is starting to crack. But as the carefully curated image begins to crumble, people are starting to ask: Has Harry been played? The relentless pursuit of victimhood, the never-ending stream of grievances, the lawsuits, the interviews where they professed they just wanted privacy while eagerly airing their private lives—it’s all starting to look a bit tiresome, isn’t it? It’s as if Meghan brings chaos and strife wherever she goes, leaving a trail of scorched earth behind her. And now, Harry, standing alone in the ashes, might be waking up to the realisation that he’s not a leading man in a romcom. He’s the fall guy in a badly scripted melodrama.

The cracks in their fortress of solidarity are hard to ignore. From awkward public appearances where Harry looks increasingly weary, to reports of them living “separate lives,” it’s clear that the Duke of Sussex’s fairytale with the duchess might not have the happy ending he envisioned. Could it be that Harry is slowly but surely realising the poison in the air? That aligning himself so completely with Meghan’s seemingly endless vendettas has isolated him from everyone who once cared for him? The court of public opinion has shifted, and not in their favour.

Perhaps Harry is beginning to understand that the woman he thought was his greatest ally may, in fact, be his Achilles heel. Meghan’s love for the spotlight is insatiable, and Harry’s been dragged along for the ride, his own identity slowly eroded. Meanwhile, she flourishes as the victim-turned-heroine in her own fantasy, playing to the gallery of sycophants while carefully casting Harry in the role of the sacrificial lamb.

As he surveys the debris of the bridges burned and relationships fractured, one can only wonder—how much longer before Harry tires of this reality show existence? The toxicity surrounding Meghan Markle has become undeniable, but the question now is: does Harry finally see it?

Ah, Meghan Markle, the Duchess of Sussex—what 𝐢𝐬 the truth beneath that glossy exterior? Is she the warm, genuine philanthropist championing change, or are we all witnessing a carefully constructed façade, where even the smiles appear as tightly rehearsed as a royal wave?

Take, for instance, the multitude of "fake smiles" reportedly flashed at every corner. Body language experts, with their magnifying glasses practically glued to her lips, have suggested these expressions seem less like joy and more like a polite veneer slapped on to mask her inner turmoil. You know the kind—the smile you give when your shoes pinch or, worse, when your multimillion-dollar Spotify deal is unceremoniously yanked from under you. 

One can’t help but wonder: Is this all part of the performance? Are we seeing the real Meghan, or is she merely playing a part? The cool, poised ex-royal who can handle the cruel blows of the public arena—or the fiery and determined woman, as some astrologers have hinted, forever grappling with balancing her public and private self?

Then there’s the curious dichotomy between her self-professed vulnerability and her undeniable confidence. She wants to be seen as relatable, yet she's working on projects bigger than Harry’s ginger beard—because make no mistake, darling, she 𝐢𝐬 the one wearing the trousers. Confidence, sure, but is it authentic? Or merely a Hollywood-esque masking of whatever emotional storms may be brewing underneath?

Whatever the case, Markle’s perpetual attempts to curate her image are unmistakable, making one wonder: Is she as real as a royal reality show, or are we merely buying tickets to a performance? 

But perhaps, like many in the public eye, the Duchess knows that keeping up appearances is part of the gig. After all, in a world where one’s entire brand can be undone with the flick of a tweet or, worse, a Netflix snub, who can blame her for wanting to manage the narrative? Still, one has to ask: at what point does the performance stop, and the real Meghan Markle begin?

Keep watching, folks. This might be the longest act yet.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle once declared their intention to step back from royal life, seeking a quieter existence away from the relentless media scrutiny, the invasive headlines, and the unending circus of royal duty. We all remember that moment in January 2020 when the world collectively gasped at their decision to break free from the gilded cage of monarchy. They wanted, they said, to live in peace. They craved privacy.

But fast forward to today, and one has to wonder—if privacy was truly the goal, why do Harry and Meghan constantly seek out the spotlight like moths to a flame? After all, we’ve hardly been short of the couple these past few years, have we? And every time we think they’re retreating into the shadows, back they come, brighter than ever, ready to tell us more, reveal more, and sell more.

When Harry and Meghan announced their “progressive new role” in early 2020, they claimed they would split their time between the UK and North America, free from the relentless scrutiny of the British press. They wanted to raise their children away from prying eyes, to live like regular people.

Well, if this is what regular people do—signing £100 million deals with Netflix—then sign me up! Because just months after their grand exit from royal life, the couple inked a lucrative contract with the streaming giant to produce documentaries, films, and television shows. Their docuseries, 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 & 𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐡𝐚𝐧, provided intimate glimpses of their lives—precisely the kind of exposure they once claimed to flee from.

One can only marvel at the paradox: “Please leave us alone,” they plead, while flinging open the doors to their California mansion, cameras rolling, lights flashing.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐩𝐫𝐚𝐡 𝐁𝐨𝐦𝐛𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐥𝐥

Ah, but we’re not done. Who can forget 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 interview with Oprah Winfrey in March 2021? Broadcast to millions across the globe, Harry and Meghan laid bare their grievances with the royal family in what was undoubtedly the most talked-about television moment of the year. Harry lamented the toxic tabloid culture that hounded them, but in the next breath, the couple dropped bombshell after bombshell that sent those very tabloids into a feeding frenzy.

Was this stepping away from the limelight? Hardly. This was stepping right into the fire—voluntarily.

 ‘𝐒𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐞’ 𝐔𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐚

As if the Oprah interview wasn’t enough, along came *Spare*, Harry’s tell-all memoir published in early 2023. Within its pages, Harry spilled secrets from the very heart of royal life—recollections of private conversations, moments of familial tension, and, oh yes, that infamous fight with his brother William. The book broke sales records but also shattered any remaining illusion that Harry and Meghan desired a quiet life. They weren’t running from the spotlight; they were standing squarely in its centre, microphone in hand, demanding more.

To promote ‘𝐒𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐞’ Harry and Meghan embarked on a media blitz, appearing on television interviews, podcasts, and talk shows—each one more revealing than the last. Privacy? This isn’t privacy. This is public relations, plain and simple.

text:
Meghan Markle: Unveiling the Dark Triad Persona
                  Any one recognize these traits?
In the realm of celebrity, few figures have divided public opinion quite like Meghan Markle. From her fairy-tale wedding into the British royal family to her subsequent departure and public revelations, Meghan has captivated global attention with a charisma that masks deeper complexities.

Psychologists often refer to the Dark Triad personality traits—narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy—as a trifecta of malevolent characteristics. Meghan Markle, through her public persona and actions, appears to embody these traits in a way that has sparked controversy and intrigue.

• Narcissism: At the core of Meghan's persona lies an unyielding self-focus and a grandiose sense of self-importance. Her journey from actress to Duchess was marked by a calculated ascent, leveraging connections and opportunities to elevate her status. The decision to step back from royal duties was framed as a quest for personal authenticity, yet critics argue it was a narcissistic act of self-preservation, disregarding centuries-old traditions and protocols for her own aspirations.

• Machiavellianism: Meghan has demonstrated a shrewd ability to navigate the intricate webs of power and influence. From her strategic media appearances to her adept handling of public relations, she has portrayed herself as a victim while subtly manipulating public opinion to her advantage. Her alliances with influential figures and calculated interviews are seen as Machiavellian maneuvers aimed at securing sympathy and support, often at the expense of others' reputations.

• Psychopathy: Beneath her polished exterior lies a cool detachment and a lack of empathy characteristic of psychopathy. Critics point to her alleged mistreatment of staff and strained relationships within the royal family as evidence of callous disregard for others' feelings. Her ability to shift narratives effortlessly, from victim to activist, without genuine remorse or accountability, underscores a chilling disregard for the emotional impact of her actions on others.

The saga of Meghan Markle serves as a cautionary tale of the Dark Triad personality at play in the public eye. Her rise and subsequent controversies illustrate the seductive allure of power and the pitfalls of unchecked ambition. As she continues to navigate her post-royal life, observers are left to ponder the lasting impact of a woman whose path to fame was paved with ambition, controversy, and a profound impact on the institution she once sought to conquer.

In the realm of celebrity psychology, Meghan Markle stands as a compelling case study—a figure whose enigmatic charm and calculated maneuvers continue to fascinate and divide public opinion. Her journey serves as a stark reminder of the complexities of human nature and the enduring allure of the Dark Triad persona in the modern age.

Prince Harry — The Pinnacle of Media Manipulation and Hypocrisy
    subtitle  ===   HARRY DO WE REALLY CARE ABOUT YOUR TODGER ?

In an era where media manipulation has become alarmingly sophisticated, one individual stands out for his audacious exploitation of the press. With a blend of hypocrisy and calculated deceit, he has used various traditional platforms to advance his personal agenda while vociferously denouncing the very media he relies upon. His actions—particularly his constant invocation of his late mother’s name, the promotion of his book *Spare*, and his recent claim about Queen Elizabeth II—reveal the depths of his moral duplicity.

His memoir ‘Spare’ exemplifies his manipulative tactics. The book portrays him as a victim of media excess and royal intrigue, with every media appearance and promotional effort designed to capitalise on his grievances. This reliance on media exposure, which he simultaneously criticises, creates a hypocritical cycle of exploitation and condemnation.

A particularly egregious example of this manipulation was his claim on the programme ‘Tabloids On Trial’. During the show, he asserted that Queen Elizabeth II—who passed away in 2022—had supported him in his campaign against the media. The audacity of invoking a deceased monarch to bolster his narrative, despite her inability to refute or clarify his claims, reveals a staggering level of moral bankruptcy. This exploitation of his grandmother’s legacy is not merely about garnering sympathy; it is a calculated effort to manipulate public perception and advance his agenda.

By persistently invoking his family’s names, he cynically leverages their legacies to lend credibility to his assertions. Exploiting deceased individuals who cannot contest his claims is a deliberate and calculated ploy to shape public sentiment. It underscores the disturbing extent to which he is willing to go to achieve his objectives, all while maintaining a façade of fighting against media injustice.

In essence, his behaviour epitomises profound hypocrisy. He denounces the press for its supposed biases while simultaneously manipulating every available outlet—to serve his own ends. His ability to distort narratives and exploit personal tragedies for personal gain reveals a troubling pattern of deception. The real question remains: how much lower will he sink in his quest for validation and revenge, regardless of the cost to truth and decency?

text:
The Duke of Sussex, our very own Prince Harry, forever ensconced in his Californian fortress of wokeness, emerges periodically to remind us of his perpetual state of existential dread. His latest missive, delivered with the gravitas of a man who believes he is one ill-advised soundbite away from Armageddon, once again revolves around his incessant fears regarding security. Yet, in this familiar narrative of peril, there lies a curious omission that even the most casual observer cannot fail to notice. 

Why, one wonders, does he never mention his dear children, those apple-cheeked cherubs who must surely feature prominently in his concerns for safety? No, in Harry's tale of impending doom, it is always Meghan, his duchess, his guiding star, who stands as the singular focus of his protective instincts. One could be forgiven for assuming that Archie and Lilibet, those innocents born into the Montecito soap opera, are perhaps spirited away to a secure undisclosed location every time Harry's security detail is the topic du jour. 

Is it possible, dare I say, that Harry's paternal instincts are overshadowed by his incessant need to shield Meghan from the predatory gaze of the paparazzi and the tabloid vultures? Or is this yet another chapter in the interminable saga of their beleaguered love story, where the perils of fame and the spectre of Diana's tragic fate are wheeled out to elicit a collective sigh from the global audience? 

In the grand theatre of their public pronouncements, one can't help but notice how the narrative is carefully scripted. Meghan is always the damsel in distress, while Harry, clad in the metaphorical armour of a modern-day Lancelot, valiantly fights off the demons of their shared notoriety. And the children? Well, perhaps they are tucked safely away in a nursery, blissfully unaware of their parents' ceaseless battle against the forces of darkness.

It's almost as if Harry's anxieties are a bespoke garment, tailored exclusively for Meghan, leaving one to wonder whether the children are considered less vulnerable, or simply less marketable, in this never-ending drama. 

But who are we to question the priorities of the Duke and Duchess? In their world, perhaps the greatest security threat is the one that jeopardises their perpetual narrative of victimhood. And in this theatre of the absurd, the children, it seems, play only a supporting role.

Once a beloved royal, Prince Harry’s fall from grace has left many questioning his motives and loyalty to the family and heritage that once defined him. Labeling his actions as a betrayal might seem melodramatic to some—but the facts paint a picture of treachery that’s hard to ignore.

Harry once held a special place in the hearts of the British public. A military man, a doting brother, and the cheeky prince who brought a breath of fresh air to Buckingham Palace. Yet, that sparkle has dimmed. The loyal prince seems to have turned his back on all that shaped him, trading royal duties for Hollywood glamour. What followed was an all-out attack on the institution that raised him.

Harry’s departure isn’t merely about a family squabble; it’s a departure from centuries of tradition, heritage, and duty. The monarchy isn’t just a family—it’s an institution steeped in history and service. By turning his back and airing grievances so publicly, Harry isn’t just defying his relatives—he’s disrespecting the legacy of the crown and its values.

The Oprah interview was a watershed moment. With shocking revelations and accusations, Harry opened the palace doors to an international audience, a move seen by many as dishonourable. His portrayal of the Royal Family as aloof and callous seemed out of place given his own enjoyment of the institution’s privileges. He and Meghan painted themselves as victims while their star rose on the back of sensationalism.

What’s harder to accept is the lack of reconciliation or regret from Harry. Instead of mending bridges, he seems content to burn them under the guise of ‘finding his truth.’ This feels less like a personal journey and more like a public spectacle.

Every family has conflicts, but this isn’t about sibling squabbles—it’s about duty. Harry’s identity was shaped by the institution he now scorns. It’s difficult to reconcile how someone with such a deep sense of duty to Queen and country could dismantle that image for self-serving publicity.

What adds insult to injury is that Harry’s titles, wealth, and platform come from the institution he now claims to have left behind. Yet, he continues to use his royal connections to stay relevant. His actions reveal a level of immaturity—an inability to manage personal struggles without dragging his family and heritage through the mud.

Ultimately, Harry’s behaviour feels less like a courageous step into a new world and more like a betrayal of the monarchy’s principles. He wasn’t just a prince—he was a symbol of continuity, tradition, and duty. His actions have eroded trust and admiration, leaving a fractured relationship and a tarnished legacy. In many ways, Prince Harry’s journey resembles a Shakespearean tragedy: a once-heroic figure, now undone by his own decisions, leaving him in the wilderness of self-imposed exile, isolated and estranged from the royal legacy he once embodied.

text:
𝐈𝐬 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐥𝐞? 

That’s the question on everyone’s lips as the Duke of Sussex slowly, and somewhat tragically, comes to grips with the storm he’s waded into. For years, the world watched with morbid curiosity as Prince Harry fell under the spell of the cable actress who seemed to promise him the kind of liberation he thought he craved. But now, it appears the fog might be lifting.

Ever since he and Meghan Markle packed up their royal obligations and moved stateside, Harry has been like a lost puppy. Yes, he’s had the bright lights of Montecito and the comforting hum of Netflix millions to keep him warm, but let’s not pretend that anything about their lives has been a fairy tale. He’s gone from being one of the most loved members of the royal family to a footnote on the latest podcast ranking. Once a cheeky, beloved prince, he now seems diminished, frequently wielding accusations against his own flesh and blood, all in the name of “truth-telling” while sporting a perpetual look of someone who's swallowed a bee.

Of course, Meghan clings to the spotlight with the fervour of someone whose star is slowly dimming. The glossy sheen she’s worked so hard to maintain is starting to crack. But as the carefully curated image begins to crumble, people are starting to ask: Has Harry been played? The relentless pursuit of victimhood, the never-ending stream of grievances, the lawsuits, the interviews where they professed they just wanted privacy while eagerly airing their private lives—it’s all starting to look a bit tiresome, isn’t it? It’s as if Meghan brings chaos and strife wherever she goes, leaving a trail of scorched earth behind her. And now, Harry, standing alone in the ashes, might be waking up to the realisation that he’s not a leading man in a romcom. He’s the fall guy in a badly scripted melodrama.

The cracks in their fortress of solidarity are hard to ignore. From awkward public appearances where Harry looks increasingly weary, to reports of them living “separate lives,” it’s clear that the Duke of Sussex’s fairytale with the duchess might not have the happy ending he envisioned. Could it be that Harry is slowly but surely realising the poison in the air? That aligning himself so completely with Meghan’s seemingly endless vendettas has isolated him from everyone who once cared for him? The court of public opinion has shifted, and not in their favour.

Perhaps Harry is beginning to understand that the woman he thought was his greatest ally may, in fact, be his Achilles heel. Meghan’s love for the spotlight is insatiable, and Harry’s been dragged along for the ride, his own identity slowly eroded. Meanwhile, she flourishes as the victim-turned-heroine in her own fantasy, playing to the gallery of sycophants while carefully casting Harry in the role of the sacrificial lamb.

As he surveys the debris of the bridges burned and relationships fractured, one can only wonder—how much longer before Harry tires of this reality show existence? The toxicity surrounding Meghan Markle has become undeniable, but the question now is: does Harry finally see it?

text:
“𝐑𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐲 𝐭𝐨 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲: 𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐮𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐱𝐞𝐬 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐨𝐬”

It’s hard to imagine a more spectacular fall from grace. Meghan Markle, a former cable TV actress, married into the British Royal Family and found herself with a title, a global platform, and all the trappings of royalty. But this wasn’t Tinseltown—there were protocols, centuries of tradition, and an expectation to serve the British people. And here’s where the Sussexes’ story shifts from fairy tale to farce.

Let's be clear: when they first announced they were stepping back, many Brits wished them luck on their new life. Their decision to seek more privacy and independence didn’t raise many eyebrows initially. But it was their behaviour afterwards that truly soured public opinion.

What they did next is the stuff of modern hubris. First came the 𝘖𝘱𝘳𝘢𝘩 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘪𝘦𝘸, a two-hour primetime spectacular where grievances were aired in the most public way possible. Meghan, who played the “𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘳” card at every turn, presented herself as a victim of a royal machine that allegedly ignored her mental health struggles. For Harry, it was a platform to lay bare years of family resentment, tarnishing the reputations of the very people who once adored him. Royalty, by its nature, thrives on discretion, loyalty, and service, but the Sussexes were out for blood—𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘪𝘳 narrative was all that mattered.

The whining didn’t stop there. Harry’s memoir 𝘚𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘦 only deepened the chasm, dragging up petty sibling squabbles with Prince William, tantrums over tiaras, and accusations that reeked of entitlement and narcissism. Once the couple cried racism and abandonment, any residual goodwill began evaporating at lightning speed.

Their behaviour screamed hypocrisy. How could they demand privacy while signing a multimillion-dollar Netflix deal to expose the very family they abandoned? Their repeated claims of victimhood wore thin—when you trade castles for Montecito mansions, it’s hard to sell yourself as oppressed. No one cared about them leaving the royal family, but they certainly cared about the Sussexes playing both sides: royal victims and Tinseltown celebrities, crying injustice while cashing in.

What’s even more damning is their irrelevance. The world has moved on. Meghan’s Spotify podcast flopped, their Netflix ventures struggled, and their post-royal projects seem like nothing more than vanity projects. Meanwhile, King Charles, William, and Catherine continue to quietly go about the business of serving the public—a stark contrast to Harry and Meghan’s continuous soap opera.

The Sussexes were handed it all, only to throw it away in a grand gesture of self-sabotage. From royal glitz to grasping at fame, their story has shifted from one of potential to one of pathos. No one forced them out, but their behaviour post-exit ensured they are never welcomed back.

In a world that seems to worship the grandiose, few individuals exemplify the essence of narcissism quite like Meghan Markle. The erstwhile actress, now the Duchess of Sussex, has turned her life into a perpetual performance, and we are all unwilling spectators in her ongoing melodrama.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫 𝐨𝐟 𝐇𝐞𝐫 𝐎𝐰𝐧 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐝𝐲: 𝐂𝐮𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤𝐬!

From the moment she entered the royal spotlight, Meghan made it clear she intended to be the headline act. The Oprah Winfrey interview was a masterclass in self-pity, shifting the focus from the monarchy to her own perceived suffering. It’s as if she believes her struggles warrant a Netflix series—a tawdry soap opera filled with tears and accusations.

𝐂𝐫𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚 𝐂𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐬: 𝐋𝐨𝐨𝐤 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐇𝐞𝐫𝐞!

Meghan has transformed the media into her personal soapbox, scripting her narrative like a desperate writer. She unleashes well-timed leaks to cast herself as the misunderstood outsider battling an archaic institution. Instead of rising to the occasion during royal turmoil, Meghan threw a tantrum on international television, crafting an image so far removed from reality it resembles fantasy.

𝐑𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩𝐬? 𝐎𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐈𝐟 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐞 𝐇𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐮𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐬𝐞!

In Meghan’s world, relationships are expendable. Her estrangement from her father and half-siblings reads like a bad drama. She keeps only those who serve her narrative, including her infamous rift with the royal family—an institution she clearly disdains. If she isn’t the centre of attention, she seems to lose interest, leaving a trail of broken connections.

𝐅𝐚𝐦𝐞: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐇𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠

Meghan’s relentless pursuit of fame is astounding. She traded royal duties for Hollywood deals faster than you can say “publicity stunt,” signing multi-million-pound contracts while lamenting her loss of privacy. Does she care for philanthropy, or is her true love the fleeting high of applause?

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐕𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐡𝐨𝐨𝐝 𝐎𝐥𝐲𝐦𝐩𝐢𝐜𝐬: 𝐆𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐌𝐞𝐝𝐚𝐥 𝐢𝐧 𝐒𝐞𝐥𝐟-𝐏𝐢𝐭𝐲

While advocating for social issues, Meghan’s approach often feels like a marketing strategy rather than genuine concern. Each speech draws more attention to her trauma than the causes she claims to support. It’s hard to take seriously a woman who has lived in palaces while positioning herself as a martyr, using her platform for personal grievances rather than the greater good.

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐒𝐞𝐥𝐟-𝐎𝐛𝐬𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 — 𝐀 𝐋𝐨𝐧𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐆𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐚𝐠𝐞

Meghan Markle serves as a cautionary tale about the perils of narcissism. In her quest for independence and recognition, she has alienated herself from those who might offer her support. It begs the question: in a world filled with adoration and applause, will she ever find the genuine connections she seems so desperately to seek? For all her talk of freedom and authenticity, Meghan remains trapped in a gilded cage of her own making, where the pursuit of fame ultimately leaves her more isolated than ever.

And while the world watches her every move, one thing is certain: Meghan Markle is the star of her own show, and it’s a performance that reveals far more about her character than she would like to admit.

What is next, stay tuned for the horror show of meg.

text:
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲:     and      Meghan      𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐁𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐍𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐯𝐞

Prince Harry, once the shining light of the royal family, has now become a figure of contempt in Britain, a man who has not only turned his back on his family but, more egregiously, sold out his country. His actions over the past few years have burned every last bridge, leaving the British public with nothing but scorn for the man who once stood shoulder to shoulder with the people.

The Oprah interview was the tipping point. It was here that Harry, complicit in silence, allowed Meghan Markle to imply that a member of the royal family had concerns about the skin colour of their son, Archie. The accusation was seismic, sending shockwaves through the UK. But what made this worse—what made it utterly unforgivable—was Harry’s inaction. His failure to stand up for his family while his ailing grandfather, Prince Philip, was in his final days showed a callous disregard for the pain it would cause. No matter the issues he may have had behind closed doors, to go on international television and sully the name of the institution that raised him was seen by many as nothing short of treachery.

And as if the Oprah debacle wasn’t bad enough, we were later subjected to 𝘏𝘢𝘳𝘳𝘺 & 𝘔𝘦𝘨𝘩𝘢𝘯, the Netflix mockumentary thinly veiled as a love letter to themselves but in truth, a very public airing of grievances. It was here that Meghan’s mocking of the royal tradition of curtsying to Queen Elizabeth shocked us Brits. With a poorly executed theatrical bow and a laughable comparison to medieval times, she belittled a gesture that symbolises respect and duty—values the British monarchy stands for. And Harry? He smirked. His silence, again, was deafening. How could any grandson, raised in the folds of such tradition, allow his wife to mock the woman who represented so much to so many?

The British people watched, aghast. That smirk—that quiet complicity—was a betrayal not just of his family, but of us, the British public who had once held him in such high regard. Queen Elizabeth, beloved and respected, was the embodiment of duty and grace, and for Harry to stand idly by as she was mocked before her passing will never be forgiven. The wound is deep, and it’s raw.

Then came the memoir 𝘚𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘦. If the Netflix series was a veiled attack, 𝘚𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘦 was an all-out assault. Page after page of grievances, personal attacks on his father and brother, intimate family moments laid bare for the world to see. The British public has always respected the monarchy’s ability to keep private matters within the palace walls. Harry tore that tradition apart. And for what? A quick buck, a bit of global attention. The title of ‘spare’ may have haunted him his whole life, but now it’s clear: the role he once resented is one he’s embraced—no longer a prince, but a spare to the very values that once defined him.

For us Brits, it isn’t just the content of his attacks that hurts—it’s the fact that he’s chosen to air them so publicly, so vindictively. The monarchy is not just his family; it is the backbone of British history, culture, and identity. To see it so easily discarded and vilified by one of its own is a wound that may never heal.

No, Britain will not forgive Harry. The man who was once the cheeky prince with a ready smile and a heart for service has become a symbol of betrayal. He has betrayed his family, his country, and his role in history. And for that, there is no going back.

Oh, the irony! Meghan Markle, our ‘favourite’ Duchess of Dismay, is reportedly working on a tell-all memoir about her alleged 72 hours as a working royal. Yes, that’s right—three days in a tiara, and she’s convinced she has enough material to rival Shakespeare’s tragedies. I can hardly wait for the enlightening tales of adversity that surely await us. Spoiler alert: I suspect they’ll be as riveting as watching paint dry.

Let’s not forget that Meghan’s grand total of royal duties could hardly fill a pamphlet, yet she’s poised to regale us with her experiences as if she survived a shipwreck. In those fleeting 72 hours, she managed to squeeze in a handful of engagements before she and Harry were off, leaving behind a trail of baffled courtiers and one very confused corgi. But alas, this is the same woman who turned a mere two years in the spotlight into an epic saga of betrayal and emotional trauma. So why stop now?

What can we expect from this memoir? A deep dive into the horrors of royal life? A gripping narrative detailing the systemic oppression she faced from her fellow royals? I can only imagine the subheadings: “Chapter One: The Cruelty of Curtsying” and “Chapter Two: The Unbearable Weight of the Crown.” Truly, who knew tiaras could be so oppressive?

If her previous forays into storytelling are anything to go by, we can anticipate another round of victimhood, complete with dramatic retellings of her time in the palace. Perhaps she’ll recount the agonising moment when she discovered the palace didn’t come with a personal stylist or how she was forced to endure the trials of royal protocol while trying to navigate a world where she was expected to smile and wave.

But let’s be real. This memoir is destined to be another whinge-fest, a victim’s manifesto penned by a woman who spent more time on Instagram than she did attending royal events. Meghan will undoubtedly fill the pages with tales of how she was misunderstood, how her mental health was allegedly jeopardised by the stuffy traditions of the monarchy, and how she was forced to endure life with “difficult” people like the Queen and Prince Charles.

And of course, no memoir of hers would be complete without the obligatory accusations of racism and systemic cruelty. It’s the get out of jail free card in her narrative, allowing her to play the role of the wronged princess in a fairytale gone horribly awry. Who knew a three-day stint could come with so many grievances?

In the end, Meghan’s memoir will likely reflect more on her relentless quest for victimhood than any real insights into the workings of the royal family. If she really believes she can turn a brief royal experience into a bestseller, then bless her heart. I’d wager my hat that it’ll be yet another saga of self-pity dressed up as profound wisdom.

So, fasten your seatbelts, Meghan Markle is about to take us on yet another wild ride through her self-crafted narrative, and I have a feeling it’s going to be one heck of a predictable journey!

text:
𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐥𝐞: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐮𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐞'𝐬 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚'𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐞𝐧

Meghan Markle, self-styled "duchess of the people," seems to have quietly elevated herself to the role of America’s queen. No tiaras, no palaces (unless Montecito counts), and no coronation. Instead, she’s created her own version of royalty, blending celebrity and titles with a hefty Netflix deal. In her mind, she’s not just part of a royal family; she is *the* royal family.

This didn’t happen overnight. From the moment she walked down the aisle at St George’s Chapel, Meghan appeared more Hollywood than Windsor. That twinkle wasn’t the glow of a new duchess embracing regal duty—it was the gleam of someone who had just landed the lead role in a global drama. But a supporting role wasn’t enough. Meghan had bigger dreams.

From the outset, she crafted herself as the archetype of modern royalty—glamorous, relatable (if you like $14 million mansions), and oppressed by a world that "didn’t understand her." Meghan isn’t interested in the pomp of Old Blighty; she craves adulation, magazine covers, and the constant spotlight. Her royalty is less about duty and more about celebrity.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐄𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐞

When Meghan and Harry left royal life for California, many thought they sought peace. Instead, they reinvented themselves as America’s answer to royalty. Setting up a multimillion-dollar media empire, they seemed to cast themselves as the new royal family of the West Coast. Meghan, especially, embraced her role as America’s princess—wronged by an archaic institution, now "finding her voice" in the land of the free.

But America already has its own royalty—Hollywood. It doesn’t follow Windsor rules; it’s ruthless, fickle, and loves a scandal more than a curated PR image. Meghan, like an ingénue, believes she can be both a Hollywood queen and a royal duchess. The trouble is, she’s not quite pulling it off.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐓𝐢𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐎𝐛𝐬𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧

Despite claiming to seek a "normal" life, Meghan clings to her royal title like a last Louis Vuitton bag on Rodeo Drive. In every appearance, she’s “the Duchess of Sussex.” Her role in American life is drenched in royal overtones—co-founding Archewell, lecturing from her Montecito mansion, and wielding her title like a sceptre.

Meghan forgets that in America, titles don’t make you royal. What works in the UK, where centuries of tradition cushion you, doesn’t fly across the Atlantic. Here, you’re only as royal as your last deal. Americans love their celebrities messy and flawed, not preachy.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐚𝐢𝐫𝐲𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐖𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐬

Meghan is obsessed with her own fairytale. Not the British royal version, but one where she’s both the damsel and heroine, escaping the clutches of an evil institution to find her true calling. She wants to be something bigger, something uniquely American—royalty on her own terms, free from tradition but full of influence.

In Meghan’s world, she’s not the failed duchess but the woman who dared to rise above royal life. She’s self-anointed as the new face of American royalty. The trouble is, in America, royalty is fleeting. Yesterday’s queen is tomorrow’s tabloid fodder.

𝐀 𝐓𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐓𝐰𝐨 𝐂𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐬

Ultimately, Meghan’s attempt to crown herself as America’s royalty may leave her stuck between two worlds. In Britain, her status is controversial; in America, she’s just another celebrity hoping for relevance in a crowded field. No title or PR stunt will cement her as true royalty in a land of Kardashians and Oprah Winfreys.

But don’t tell Meghan that. In her mind, she’s already America’s queen. Now, she just needs the world to agree.

text:
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐥𝐞𝐬 

Allow me a moment of reflection—a moment to thank South Park for saying, in blunt cartoon form, what we’ve all been thinking for far too long. It took a pair of animated misfits to finally unmask the Sussexes as the preening, privacy-loving paradoxes they are. And there they were: Harry, the wide-eyed prince who traded a crown for celebrity handshakes, and Meghan, the self-styled activist whose causes seem to end where the camera cuts. In one fell swoop, 𝘚𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘩 𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘬 delivered what the world had been silently begging for: a full-throttle takedown of the Southparkles and their spectacular descent into self-parody.

Remember when these two high-tailed it out of Britain, bemoaning the shackles of royal life, only to shove their brand into every screen from Montecito to Manhattan? The escape to “freedom” quickly turned into a relentless self-promotional tour, complete with a glossy Netflix deal, weepy docu-series, and a Spotify podcast that droned on as vapidly as the platitudes they preach. Privacy, it turns out, is a state of mind—for the Sussexes, it’s one they scream about from every headline, podcast, and interview, their own echo chamber of self-pity.

𝘚𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘩 𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘬 didn’t invent this farce; it merely held up a merciless mirror. They nailed Harry’s unearned martyrdom and Meghan’s shapeshifting causes, two perfectly polished caricatures of victimhood turned luxury brand. And what do the ‘Southparkles’ do in response? More finger-pointing, more grievances, another episode of “How the Palace Wronged Us,” as if the world hadn’t long ago tuned out. The Queen managed seventy years of scrutiny with grace, but two years of negative press have Harry and Meghan running to their lawyers—confirming that, yes, the only thing they’re actually good at is complaining.

In truth, 𝘚𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘩 𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘬 gave them a rare gift: the one thing that’s been missing in the echo chamber of their own making—perspective. But, of course, Harry and Meghan can’t see the humour. The irony is so thick you could spread it on toast: two people who desperately crave the spotlight, now reduced to cartoon characters in the cultural joke they can’t escape. Perhaps they should finally do us all a favour and give us the one thing they promised but never delivered—a quiet exit. Then again, where would the profit be in that?

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐮𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐱 𝐄𝐦𝐩𝐢𝐫𝐞: 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐭 𝐨𝐧 𝐆𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞, 𝐓𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐝

In the latest chapter of the Sussexes’ post-palace saga, the power couple known for “escaping” the royal family’s golden cage seems to have run into a bit of a gilded problem of their own. Enter 𝘐𝘯𝘛𝘰𝘶𝘤𝘩’s newest headline: “𝘋𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘰𝘺𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘺 𝘎𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘥!”—not exactly the fairy-tale ending they had in mind when they departed Britain’s shores, proclamations of independence trailing behind them.

Let’s dissect this “$100 million empire collapse,” shall we? For two people who once bemoaned the scrutiny and pressures of being in the royal fishbowl, Harry and Meghan sure seemed to make a swift U-turn back into the spotlight, albeit a more lucrative one. Who knew privacy could be so profitable? Between lucrative Netflix deals, star-studded Spotify podcasts, and tell-all book advances, they proved that fame can indeed be sold by the pound—until, it appears, the empire built on grievances and carefully crafted victimhood narratives began showing some cracks.

“𝘈𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘉𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘴! screams the subhead, as if the world needed reminding of their extravagances. For Harry, the young prince who once dared to tell the world his father had financially abandoned him (while living in a multimillion-dollar Montecito mansion), financial reality may now be arriving with the grace of a stagecoach collision. As for Meghan, the transformation from a self-styled humanitarian to the Duchess of Dollar Signs has not exactly gone unnoticed.

And now, it seems, the “reckless royals” have reached the inevitable end of their fairy tale: not with the pomp and pageantry they once denounced, but with headlines about their “𝘈𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘴!” Yes, the allure of billionaire ambitions was just too tantalising to resist, even for those who claimed to be fleeing the trappings of aristocratic privilege. One might say their undoing wasn’t so much greed as a relentless pursuit of relevance—wrapped in the velvet of luxury and sprinkled with a hint of delusion.

So, as the Sussex empire teeters, perhaps this isn’t the fairy tale they envisioned when they traded Buckingham Palace for a Californian castle. Instead of newfound freedom, it seems they’ve simply exchanged one gilded cage for another—only this time, the bars are forged by ambition, avarice, and a ravenous pursuit of fame.

Oh, the irony. Here we have the Duke and Duchess of Sussex—those self-styled champions of “privacy” who fled the royal fold to pursue their “authentic” lives—caught in the act of their true pursuit: piles upon piles of cash. Prince Harry, grinning like a Cheshire cat, cracks a whip with all the enthusiasm of a ringmaster orchestrating his own spectacle, while Meghan clutches a bulging sack of money, her grin an unmistakable sign of how far she’s come from cable TV to the centre of a money-making circus.

And lying beneath this grand parade, the ghostly presence of Princess Diana—“The People’s Princess”—whose memory Harry has used justify his treachery. The very mother he claims to honour, positioned here as a quiet, helpless spectator in the spectacle he’s made of her legacy. Diana, who genuinely connected with people and dedicated herself to causes that meant something, now finds her image entangled in the cash-fuelled carnival Harry and Meghan have orchestrated in her name.

With banknotes and gold coins cascading like confetti, you can practically hear the ka-ching echoing through Montecito. From Netflix docuseries to tell-all memoirs, the Sussex duo has turned “public service” into “personal profit.” Privacy? They only wanted privacy from the obligations, it seems—not from the cash and cameras that come with the royal titles they claim to despise.

If Diana were here, she’d give her son a royal dressing-down for exploiting her memory to line his own pockets. Because for all Harry’s posturing, he’s not walking in his mother’s footsteps; he’s trampling on her memory.

text:
𝐀 𝐌𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐭𝐨𝐫: 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲’𝐬 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐇𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲

Prince Harry, the lad who once charmed a nation, has managed quite the transformation: from beloved royal to poster boy for betrayal. In centuries past, he’d be dragged to the Tower with little ceremony, his name whispered with distaste over tankards of ale. Today, he basks in California sunshine, preaching authenticity while ghosting the very traditions that made him. Truly, a modern traitor for modern times.

For what else could we call a prince who has traded his duty for Netflix deals, swapped family loyalty for public therapy sessions, and thrown his heritage to the wind in favour of a victim narrative? Picture it: Harry, once a soldier in Afghanistan, now waging a different sort of war—a tireless battle against his own past, as he sits in his Montecito mansion. Gone are the days of duty and decorum; now it’s all about the next “revelation,” the next family gripe aired to anyone still willing to listen.

Of course, there’s Meghan, sharing in this saga as if they’re star-crossed lovers in a production of 𝘙𝘰𝘮𝘦𝘰 𝘢𝘯𝘥 𝘑𝘶𝘭𝘪𝘦𝘵: 𝘛𝘩𝘦 𝘎𝘳𝘪𝘦𝘷𝘢𝘯𝘤𝘦 𝘠𝘦𝘢𝘳𝘴. Together, they’ve built an empire on carefully curated angst, dressing up their defection as a noble quest for “freedom.” And yet, one can’t help but wonder if Harry’s “freedom” really amounts to little more than a gilded cage of their own making.

Meanwhile, back in Britain, Prince William quietly shoulders the legacy Harry discarded, preparing himself for kingship. His royal path is steady, measured—a role fulfilled with grace. Harry, on the other hand, seems more determined to stamp his name as a rogue prince, thumbing his nose at history as he clings to the fleeting rewards of his rebellion.

If Harry hoped to cement himself as some romantic figure, a maverick hero for the ages, he’s sorely mistaken. Instead, he’s  joined a long list of deserters and disgraced figures, his place in history etched not with respect but with regret. Because at the end of the day, there’s little noble in betrayal, no honour in disloyalty, and no lasting glory in the desertion of one’s own family. For a modern prince, he’s carved out a legacy steeped in treachery—one that history will neither forget nor forgive.

𝐀 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐓𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫: 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲’𝐬 𝐓𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐖𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐇𝐢𝐦 𝐢𝐧 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬

If we were to transpose Prince Harry’s behaviour to the time of our ancestors, the boy would find himself not in the opulent halls of a palace but rather in the dank confines of the Tower of London, languishing in chains. For in a bygone age, when treachery was dealt with by more than just the dubious appeasement of public opinion, he would have been dispatched to the tower quicker than you can say ‘traitor.’

Imagine the scene: a raucous court, gossip swirling like smoke from a Tudor fireplace. The nobles, their heads adorned with plumed hats, would shake their heads in disbelief, horrified at Harry’s audacity. This is a man who has squandered his royal birthright on a flimsy narrative of self-pity and the incessant drone of ‘me, me, me.’ Once the darling of the nation, he has plunged from grace faster than one of his cringe-inducing lectures.

The Tower, with its grim history of imprisoning those who dared to defy the crown, would be a fitting abode for our runaway prince. Here, amidst the echo of clanking chains and the occasional crow of a raven perched on the battlements, he would reflect on his many misdeeds—turning his back on a family steeped in tradition and duty. It is no exaggeration to say that he has become a masterclass in public disgrace, with a Netflix contract in hand and a penchant for revealing family secrets like a particularly scandalous Victorian novel.

Let us not forget the allies he has chosen—his wife, who seems intent on making headlines as though they were some sort of royalty-obsessed Kardashians, and a media machine that churns out sympathy pieces like a factory line of self-serving narratives. In the days of yore, such behaviour would have led to a one-way ticket to the Tower, where the only entertainment would be the occasional visit from the executioner, brandishing his axe with the same disdain the British public now holds for the Sussexes.

And who could blame us? Harry’s relentless parade of grievances—his childhood traumas, his estranged family, his perpetual victimhood—has grown tiresome. It feels as if he has taken the lessons of his late mother, Princess Diana, and turned them into a sordid reality show, where every episode is marked by betrayal and an insatiable need for public approval. One might argue that Diana, had she been around, would have given him a stern talking-to, perhaps even a ‘get a grip, Harry’ lecture over a cup of tea.

As he and Meghan traipse around the globe, preaching the virtues of mental health while simultaneously making a mockery of their own familial ties, one can’t help but wonder if their antics might prompt a royal edict—‘Let them eat cake’ as they sit in their ivory tower, oblivious to the discontent brewing below. For in this land of pomp and pageantry, where tradition is revered, their antics are as out of place as a jester in a cathedral.

Ultimately, Harry won’t find himself in the Tower, but perhaps it’s time to ponder the legacy he is crafting for himself—one of disgrace rather than distinction. In a world that once revered him, he now stands as a cautionary tale, a prince turned pauper of public opinion. It’s a royal disgrace that would make any self-respecting Prince shudder in their boots. If only he could hear the whispers of history echoing through the stone walls, reminding him that treachery, once committed, has a way of finding its just desserts.

He has disgraced himself as well as his family.

Prince Harry’s downfall is a masterclass in how to squander a royal legacy, trading duty for self-pity and fame for victimhood. Once a beloved prince, now he’s more like a tabloid caricature—a man perpetually aggrieved, endlessly fixated on a narrative of blame. The tragic irony? He’s the architect of his own demise.

After the spectacular mess that was 𝘔𝘦𝘨𝘹𝘪𝘵, Harry and Meghan promised they were stepping back for a quiet life away from the suffocating grip of royal duties. But what followed wasn’t a retreat to the countryside—it was a relentless assault on the monarchy. In his memoir 𝘚𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘦, Harry exposed the royal family’s private affairs in a way that felt less like a heartfelt confession and more like a glorified tantrum. From physical altercations with William to tales of being denied “extra sausages” at breakfast and the horror of a smaller bedroom, Harry’s grievances came off as the petulant cries of a man unable to cope with the reality of his privileged existence. His anecdotes about being deprived of a lavish lifestyle, including the shocking detail that King Charles had cut off his pocket money, painted a picture of someone intent on airing family laundry while completely missing the mark on what it means to struggle.

Not only has the British public had enough, but more people globally are seeing him in his true colours. What was once endearing—the cheeky lad in the military, the prince who walked behind his mother’s coffin with quiet dignity—has now morphed into a man perpetually at war with his own privilege. His complaints, whether about family squabbles or being told Meghan had to earn her keep, are so far removed from reality that they seem almost satirical. The grand irony, of course, is that for someone so intent on escaping the royal spotlight, Harry seems desperate to cling onto any fragment of it that remains.

The cracks in the Sussex facade are now painfully obvious. Once a united front, Harry is now appearing alone more frequently, sparking speculation that even his marriage isn’t immune to the fallout of their disastrous PR. Meghan, once touted as the modern, progressive breath of fresh air, is increasingly seen as a catalyst in Harry’s undoing—a figure whose Hollywood aspirations and woke crusades have done little but alienate her from the public she so desperately sought approval from.

Harry’s story isn’t one of triumph over adversity; it’s a cautionary tale of self-sabotage. In his quest to escape the clutches of the monarchy, he’s become more of a prisoner than ever—trapped by his own choices, his once-promising legacy reduced to little more than a footnote in royal history. And the sad truth is, the more he whinges and wallows, the less anyone seems to care.
