author: @kansasrose2909
text:
Why    Does Meghan Markle Want Us To Hate Her?   
There are plenty of reasons to hate Meghan Markle, so why did she just give us a whole Netflix season of more ammo? From stabbing the royal family in the back after having her entire life subsidized by British taxpayers to earning $25 million from Spotify for a few middling podcast episodes, Markle is a villainous figure who rakes in hate, not the praise and fandom she is clearly desperate for.

When Markle made her grand return to Instagram this New Year after dramatically quitting social media in 2021, it wasn’t for funsies. It was to announce and promote her new eight-part Netflix show, “With Love, Meghan.” 
From the teaser trailer she shared, the series appears to be Markle’s best attempt at LARPing Martha Stewart with her celebrity pals on her $15 million Montecito compound. “I’m going to share some tips and tricks,” Markle says as she peruses the flower market and sprinkles dried flowers on top of glazed donuts.

“We’re not in the pursuit of perfection. We’re in the pursuit of joy!” she exclaims with an acute degree of inauthenticity. The copy is dripping with feigned platitudes and the images are suspiciously rife with royal ripoffs. This trailer is so cringe-inducing that it physically makes my eyes twitch.

What’s most surprising about this product is that there was no one close enough to her to wave their hands and gently guide her in the complete opposite direction. When Netflix came knocking, what pitches did she turn down when she opted for this Ballerina Farm wannabe vanity project? Did no one who loves her suggest a series with a bit more sympathetic angle? A reality show where she helps down-and-out folks find a new home? A docu-series where she visits small, but beautiful American cities, highlighting everyday heroes?

I’m just shooting from the hip, and these may not be streaming hits, but the fact that no one close to her advised her against her casual yet glamourous homemaker shtick (or they did and she didn’t listen) says a lot about the type of person she surrounds herself with. Ironically, that’s also what we mainly learn from the teaser trailer guest list — that Markle spends her time arranging flowers and beekeeping with some of the most affluent and out-of-touch celebrities in her Hollywood bubble. “This is probably one of the most glamourous moments of my life,” gushes Mindy Kaling.

And it’s important to clarify here that the snobbery does not come from the idea of picture-perfect homemaking. This type of nearly unattainable farm-to-table perfection is what skyrocketed and sustained Martha Stewart, Ina Garten, Ballerina Farm, and waves of Instagram influencers following in their footsteps. Women do not loathe these women for their ideas or talents. We gobble them up and strive to emulate their recipes and cabinet paint colors in our own kitchens. No, it’s the laughable idea that the privileged princess, the Hollywood actress-turned-diva-sister-in-law, and royal golddigger who excommunicated her husband from his family, is someone we trust as a source for bringing joy and life into our own homes.

The only plausible explanation for Markle’s vanity project is that she relishes victimhood so much that she doesn’t care what the haters say because their critiques and comments sustain her signature victim mentality. Knowing she will never be the beloved people’s princess like her late mother-in-law, she’s stopped trying and settled for the loathed queen of Montecito.

⚠Warning: The cringe level is off the charts! 

Meghan Markle has turned her need for control into a public spectacle, constantly reminding both Harry—and the world—who’s really in charge. The so-called 'independent feminist' has manipulated and emasculated her husband to the point where he’s convinced he needs her, not the other way around. Every public appearance becomes a desperate display of clinging and clutching, as she makes sure no one forgets who’s pulling the strings in their ‘power couple’ dynamic. 

Her inability to keep her hands to herself, especially in professional settings, shatters her claims of being independent. Instead, it highlights just how dependent she is on Harry’s status. Meghan knows her place in the spotlight is fragile at best, and she overcompensates by diminishing Harry’s shine, even at events meant to honor him. This isn’t just insecurity on display; it’s a calculated effort to keep him under her control, ensuring he never thinks for himself or steals the spotlight. 

Her opportunistic tendencies have earned her quite the reputation. Meghan clings onto anyone she can use to her advantage, and this has become well-known in Hollywood circles. It’s one of the many reasons no one’s calling her for collaborations, scripts, or deals. Designers avoid her, and she’s seen as difficult, selfish, and entitled, all while believing she’s far more important than she really is—just because she managed to convince a clueless prince to marry her. 

The truth is, her constant need to cling to Harry—both literally and figuratively—reveals her desperation to stay relevant. Without Harry, there’s no royal status, no spotlight, and certainly no fortune to fall back on. Her every touch is a reminder that she’s not just grasping for love; she’s securing her bank account. Her ‘affection’ is nothing more than a thinly veiled tactic to keep Harry in line, making sure he doesn’t wander off or—heaven forbid—get influenced by anyone else. 

So, the next time you see her awkwardly draping herself over Harry or invading the personal space of others, know that it’s not just bad manners—it’s her way to try and hold onto what she craves the most: fame. Meghan’s fame is tied to Harry and is because of Harry, and her grip on him is as much about control as it is about holding onto her only shot at staying relevant. 

A hand on Harry? That’s not love—it’s a desperate move to keep her lottery ticket firmly in hand. And trust me, it’s as transparent as her PR stunts. Enjoy this montage of Meghan's cringe-worthy, over-the-top attempts to hold onto relevance—one awkward grasp at a time. 📣 👠DICTATOR IN HIGH HEELS: Meghan Markle’s Reign of Hypocrisy Exposed – From Empowerment Icon to Ruthless Boss 📣⚠

Meghan Markle has mastered the art of portraying herself as the perpetual victim, but a closer look at the mounting reports paints a very different picture. Described as a “dictator in high heels,” Meghan is allegedly ruthless behind the scenes, belittling staff, demanding total control, and reducing grown men to tears. While she loves to present herself as a beacon of empowerment, compassion, and inclusivity, the reality seems far removed from the buzzwords she so often champions. 

Her hypocrisy becomes evident when we compare her public pleas for sympathy to the way she treats those around her. Meghan cries victimhood, particularly during her pregnancies, when she claimed to have been "cruelly" bullied online. Yet, the same woman who claims to stand against bullying has been accused multiple times of doing exactly that—bullying her staff into submission and creating a toxic environment so unbearable that even seasoned professionals have fled. 

As YT's Martin DeCoder points out, “Meghan has a habit of defending herself under the guise of speaking for everyone and the group she's desperately trying to constitute. Her rhetoric isn't freeing or empowering—it’s designed to keep people in their place.” She frequently monopolizes terms like "freedom," "compassion," and "inclusivity," but they’re just tools for her to manipulate the narrative and paint herself as a victim in the court of public opinion. Interviews with preordained victim sympathizers, like Oprah, serve as platforms where Meghan oversimplifies and reframes any valid criticism as "bullying." 

And let's not forget Prince Harry, who is often described as a passive enabler in all of this. While Meghan's relentless control is well-documented, Harry’s role as her “charming” but complicit counterpart should not be overlooked. Time and again, the couple has made impulsive, chaotic decisions—whether it's breaking ties with the royal family or burning bridges in Hollywood—and Harry, though less criticized, is certainly no innocent bystander. 

The irony in all of this is hard to miss: Meghan, who preaches empowerment, is allegedly anything but empowering to those who have the misfortune of working for her. She has mastered the victim narrative, manipulating every platform she gets to sidestep accountability while conveniently playing the role of a woman under attack. But the constant churn of staff, the public resignations, and now the latest accusations all point to one undeniable fact—Meghan is far more "dictator" than "duchess." 

In the end, Meghan’s carefully constructed image is collapsing under the weight of her own actions. She may continue to paint herself as a crusader for equity and justice, but the truth is, she seems far more interested in protecting her own image at the expense of others. As more evidence surfaces, it’s becoming clear that the real story isn’t about a victim—it’s about a woman whose thirst for power and control knows no bounds. 💥

text:
Meghan Markle: Unveiling the Dark Triad Persona

In the realm of celebrity, few figures have divided public opinion quite like Meghan Markle. From her fairy-tale wedding into the British royal family to her subsequent departure and public revelations, Meghan has captivated global attention with a charisma that masks deeper complexities.

Psychologists often refer to the Dark Triad personality traits—narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy—as a trifecta of malevolent characteristics. Meghan Markle, through her public persona and actions, appears to embody these traits in a way that has sparked controversy and intrigue.

• Narcissism: At the core of Meghan's persona lies an unyielding self-focus and a grandiose sense of self-importance. Her journey from actress to Duchess was marked by a calculated ascent, leveraging connections and opportunities to elevate her status. The decision to step back from royal duties was framed as a quest for personal authenticity, yet critics argue it was a narcissistic act of self-preservation, disregarding centuries-old traditions and protocols for her own aspirations.

• Machiavellianism: Meghan has demonstrated a shrewd ability to navigate the intricate webs of power and influence. From her strategic media appearances to her adept handling of public relations, she has portrayed herself as a victim while subtly manipulating public opinion to her advantage. Her alliances with influential figures and calculated interviews are seen as Machiavellian maneuvers aimed at securing sympathy and support, often at the expense of others' reputations.

• Psychopathy: Beneath her polished exterior lies a cool detachment and a lack of empathy characteristic of psychopathy. Critics point to her alleged mistreatment of staff and strained relationships within the royal family as evidence of callous disregard for others' feelings. Her ability to shift narratives effortlessly, from victim to activist, without genuine remorse or accountability, underscores a chilling disregard for the emotional impact of her actions on others.

The saga of Meghan Markle serves as a cautionary tale of the Dark Triad personality at play in the public eye. Her rise and subsequent controversies illustrate the seductive allure of power and the pitfalls of unchecked ambition. As she continues to navigate her post-royal life, observers are left to ponder the lasting impact of a woman whose path to fame was paved with ambition, controversy, and a profound impact on the institution she once sought to conquer.

In the realm of celebrity psychology, Meghan Markle stands as a compelling case study—a figure whose enigmatic charm and calculated maneuvers continue to fascinate and divide public opinion. Her journey serves as a stark reminder of the complexities of human nature and the enduring allure of the Dark Triad persona in the modern age.

⚠ The Decline of the Invictus Games: From Respected Platform to PR Stunt ‼ 

Let’s be honest—what was once a meaningful and respected initiative has turned into a shameless PR parade, thanks to the Man-Child Harry and his D-List Social Climber wife Meghan Markle. The Invictus Games, originally created to honor and empower wounded service members, have been hijacked by a couple who seem far more interested in promoting themselves than the cause.  

Instead of focusing on veterans, the Games have become Meghan’s designer-clad runway, complete with shallow photo ops that scream “Look at me!” more than “Support our heroes.” The mission of Invictus—celebrating resilience and unity—has been overshadowed by a vanity project designed to boost their tarnished reputations. It’s insulting to the veterans who deserved better than to be props in this spectacle.  

And now, Harry wants to bring Invictus into schools? Spare us. His Vancouver appearance to promote the “Invictus Games School Program” wasn’t about inspiring kids—it was another desperate ploy to fix his approval ratings. Let’s not pretend this is about “the next generation.” This is about Harry trying to make himself look good while ignoring the obvious: his credibility is in the gutter.  

The irony is rich. Harry—privileged, out of touch, and with zero real-world experience—lecturing us about service, family, and children? No thanks. Veterans and parents alike are fed up with his constant preaching. And using kids as a PR shield to deflect from the Games’ declining support? That’s a new low. Here’s a message for Harry: LEAVE OUR KIDS ALONE! 

The Invictus Games used to stand for something noble—a symbol of respect for those who served. Now it’s bogged down by financial mismanagement, trust issues, and the polarizing presence of this fame-hungry duo. Veterans deserve so much better than having their platform co-opted by a Man-Child and his Social Climber wife, who shamelessly exploit their sacrifices to stay relevant.  

It’s time for Invictus to return to its roots: empowering veterans—not boosting the egos of those who have tarnished its cause. Enough is enough.

After years of selling grievances and unsubstantiated stories about the British Royal Family for a quick payday, they've found themselves on the outer edges of both public favour and the elite social circles they desperately wish to join. The American A-listers—the very people they had hoped to rub shoulders with—now see them for what they are: a liability. Trust is a currency they’ve long spent, and with every burned bridge, their chances of regaining any credibility or influence dwindle.

Their attempts to present themselves as victims have backfired spectacularly. Instead of garnering sympathy, they’ve managed to alienate almost everyone who once supported them. Their family, once a powerful asset, is now a distant memory—thanks largely to their own efforts. It’s almost as if they've forgotten that you can't have it both ways: you can't burn your bridges and expect them to hold up the moment you need a favour.

It’s not just that they’ve alienated their own family—by now, that's practically a given—but they’ve managed to ostracise themselves from the kind of society they crave. Meghan Markle: Unveiling the Dark Triad Persona

In the realm of celebrity, few figures have divided public opinion quite like Meghan Markle. From her fairy-tale wedding into the British royal family to her subsequent departure and public revelations, Meghan has captivated global attention with a charisma that masks deeper complexities.

Psychologists often refer to the Dark Triad personality traits—narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy—as a trifecta of malevolent characteristics. Meghan Markle, through her public persona and actions, appears to embody these traits in a way that has sparked controversy and intrigue.

• Narcissism: At the core of Meghan's persona lies an unyielding self-focus and a grandiose sense of self-importance. Her journey from actress to Duchess was marked by a calculated ascent, leveraging connections and opportunities to elevate her status. The decision to step back from royal duties was framed as a quest for personal authenticity, yet critics argue it was a narcissistic act of self-preservation, disregarding centuries-old traditions and protocols for her own aspirations.

• Machiavellianism: Meghan has demonstrated a shrewd ability to navigate the intricate webs of power and influence. From her strategic media appearances to her adept handling of public relations, she has portrayed herself as a victim while subtly manipulating public opinion to her advantage. Her alliances with influential figures and calculated interviews are seen as Machiavellian maneuvers aimed at securing sympathy and support, often at the expense of others' reputations.

• Psychopathy: Beneath her polished exterior lies a cool detachment and a lack of empathy characteristic of psychopathy. Critics point to her alleged mistreatment of staff and strained relationships within the royal family as evidence of callous disregard for others' feelings. Her ability to shift narratives effortlessly, from victim to activist, without genuine remorse or accountability, underscores a chilling disregard for the emotional impact of her actions on others.

The saga of Meghan Markle serves as a cautionary tale of the Dark Triad personality at play in the public eye. Her rise and subsequent controversies illustrate the seductive allure of power and the pitfalls of unchecked ambition. As she continues to navigate her post-royal life, observers are left to ponder the lasting impact of a woman whose path to fame was paved with ambition, controversy, and a profound impact on the institution she once sought to conquer.

In the realm of celebrity psychology, Meghan Markle stands as a compelling case study—a figure whose enigmatic charm and calculated maneuvers continue to fascinate and divide public opinion. Her journey serves as a stark reminder of the complexities of human nature and the enduring allure of the Dark Triad persona in the modern age.

𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐥𝐞: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐮𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐖𝐡𝐨 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐬 𝐒𝐡𝐞'𝐬 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚'𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐞𝐧

Meghan Markle, self-styled "duchess of the people," seems to have quietly elevated herself to the role of America’s queen. No tiaras, no palaces (unless Montecito counts), and no coronation. Instead, she’s created her own version of royalty, blending celebrity and titles with a hefty Netflix deal. In her mind, she’s not just part of a royal family; she is *the* royal family.

This didn’t happen overnight. From the moment she walked down the aisle at St George’s Chapel, Meghan appeared more Hollywood than Windsor. That twinkle wasn’t the glow of a new duchess embracing regal duty—it was the gleam of someone who had just landed the lead role in a global drama. But a supporting role wasn’t enough. Meghan had bigger dreams.

From the outset, she crafted herself as the archetype of modern royalty—glamorous, relatable (if you like $14 million mansions), and oppressed by a world that "didn’t understand her." Meghan isn’t interested in the pomp of Old Blighty; she craves adulation, magazine covers, and the constant spotlight. Her royalty is less about duty and more about celebrity.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐄𝐬𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐞

When Meghan and Harry left royal life for California, many thought they sought peace. Instead, they reinvented themselves as America’s answer to royalty. Setting up a multimillion-dollar media empire, they seemed to cast themselves as the new royal family of the West Coast. Meghan, especially, embraced her role as America’s princess—wronged by an archaic institution, now "finding her voice" in the land of the free.

But America already has its own royalty—Hollywood. It doesn’t follow Windsor rules; it’s ruthless, fickle, and loves a scandal more than a curated PR image. Meghan, like an ingénue, believes she can be both a Hollywood queen and a royal duchess. The trouble is, she’s not quite pulling it off.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐓𝐢𝐭𝐥𝐞 𝐎𝐛𝐬𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧

Despite claiming to seek a "normal" life, Meghan clings to her royal title like a last Louis Vuitton bag on Rodeo Drive. In every appearance, she’s “the Duchess of Sussex.” Her role in American life is drenched in royal overtones—co-founding Archewell, lecturing from her Montecito mansion, and wielding her title like a sceptre.

Meghan forgets that in America, titles don’t make you royal. What works in the UK, where centuries of tradition cushion you, doesn’t fly across the Atlantic. Here, you’re only as royal as your last deal. Americans love their celebrities messy and flawed, not preachy.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐚𝐢𝐫𝐲𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐖𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐬

Meghan is obsessed with her own fairytale. Not the British royal version, but one where she’s both the damsel and heroine, escaping the clutches of an evil institution to find her true calling. She wants to be something bigger, something uniquely American—royalty on her own terms, free from tradition but full of influence.

In Meghan’s world, she’s not the failed duchess but the woman who dared to rise above royal life. She’s self-anointed as the new face of American royalty. The trouble is, in America, royalty is fleeting. Yesterday’s queen is tomorrow’s tabloid fodder.

𝐀 𝐓𝐚𝐥𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐓𝐰𝐨 𝐂𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐧𝐬

Ultimately, Meghan’s attempt to crown herself as America’s royalty may leave her stuck between two worlds. In Britain, her status is controversial; in America, she’s just another celebrity hoping for relevance in a crowded field. No title or PR stunt will cement her as true royalty in a land of Kardashians and Oprah Winfreys.

But don’t tell Meghan that. In her mind, she’s already America’s queen. Now, she just needs the world to agree.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐥𝐞𝐬 

Allow me a moment of reflection—a moment to thank South Park for saying, in blunt cartoon form, what we’ve all been thinking for far too long. It took a pair of animated misfits to finally unmask the Sussexes as the preening, privacy-loving paradoxes they are. And there they were: Harry, the wide-eyed prince who traded a crown for celebrity handshakes, and Meghan, the self-styled activist whose causes seem to end where the camera cuts. In one fell swoop, 𝘚𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘩 𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘬 delivered what the world had been silently begging for: a full-throttle takedown of the Southparkles and their spectacular descent into self-parody.

Remember when these two high-tailed it out of Britain, bemoaning the shackles of royal life, only to shove their brand into every screen from Montecito to Manhattan? The escape to “freedom” quickly turned into a relentless self-promotional tour, complete with a glossy Netflix deal, weepy docu-series, and a Spotify podcast that droned on as vapidly as the platitudes they preach. Privacy, it turns out, is a state of mind—for the Sussexes, it’s one they scream about from every headline, podcast, and interview, their own echo chamber of self-pity.

𝘚𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘩 𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘬 didn’t invent this farce; it merely held up a merciless mirror. They nailed Harry’s unearned martyrdom and Meghan’s shapeshifting causes, two perfectly polished caricatures of victimhood turned luxury brand. And what do the ‘Southparkles’ do in response? More finger-pointing, more grievances, another episode of “How the Palace Wronged Us,” as if the world hadn’t long ago tuned out. The Queen managed seventy years of scrutiny with grace, but two years of negative press have Harry and Meghan running to their lawyers—confirming that, yes, the only thing they’re actually good at is complaining.

Oh, the irony. Here we have the Duke and Duchess of Sussex—those self-styled champions of “privacy” who fled the royal fold to pursue their “authentic” lives—caught in the act of their true pursuit: piles upon piles of cash. Prince Harry, grinning like a Cheshire cat, cracks a whip with all the enthusiasm of a ringmaster orchestrating his own spectacle, while Meghan clutches a bulging sack of money, her grin an unmistakable sign of how far she’s come from cable TV to the centre of a money-making circus.

And lying beneath this grand parade, the ghostly presence of Princess Diana—“The People’s Princess”—whose memory Harry has used justify his treachery. The very mother he claims to honour, positioned here as a quiet, helpless spectator in the spectacle he’s made of her legacy. Diana, who genuinely connected with people and dedicated herself to causes that meant something, now finds her image entangled in the cash-fuelled carnival Harry and Meghan have orchestrated in her name.

With banknotes and gold coins cascading like confetti, you can practically hear the ka-ching echoing through Montecito. From Netflix docuseries to tell-all memoirs, the Sussex duo has turned “public service” into “personal profit.” Privacy? They only wanted privacy from the obligations, it seems—not from the cash and cameras that come with the royal titles they claim to despise.

If Diana were here, she’d give her son a royal dressing-down for exploiting her memory to line his own pockets. Because for all Harry’s posturing, he’s not walking in his mother’s footsteps; he’s trampling on her memory.

In centuries past, he’d be dragged to the Tower with little ceremony, his name whispered with distaste over tankards of ale. Today, he basks in California sunshine, preaching authenticity while ghosting the very traditions that made him. Truly, a modern traitor for modern times.

For what else could we call a prince who has traded his duty for Netflix deals, swapped family loyalty for public therapy sessions, and thrown his heritage to the wind in favour of a victim narrative? Picture it: Harry, once a soldier in Afghanistan, now waging a different sort of war—a tireless battle against his own past, as he sits in his Montecito mansion. Gone are the days of duty and decorum; now it’s all about the next “revelation,” the next family gripe aired to anyone still willing to listen.

𝐀 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐓𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫: 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲’𝐬 𝐓𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐖𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐋𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐇𝐢𝐦 𝐢𝐧 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬

If we were to transpose Prince Harry’s behaviour to the time of our ancestors, the boy would find himself not in the opulent halls of a palace but rather in the dank confines of the Tower of London, languishing in chains. For in a bygone age, when treachery was dealt with by more than just the dubious appeasement of public opinion, he would have been dispatched to the tower quicker than you can say ‘traitor.’

Imagine the scene: a raucous court, gossip swirling like smoke from a Tudor fireplace. The nobles, their heads adorned with plumed hats, would shake their heads in disbelief, horrified at Harry’s audacity. This is a man who has squandered his royal birthright on a flimsy narrative of self-pity and the incessant drone of ‘me, me, me.’ Once the darling of the nation, he has plunged from grace faster than one of his cringe-inducing lectures.

The Tower, with its grim history of imprisoning those who dared to defy the crown, would be a fitting abode for our runaway prince. Here, amidst the echo of clanking chains and the occasional crow of a raven perched on the battlements, he would reflect on his many misdeeds—turning his back on a family steeped in tradition and duty. It is no exaggeration to say that he has become a masterclass in public disgrace, with a Netflix contract in hand and a penchant for revealing family secrets like a particularly scandalous Victorian novel.

Let us not forget the allies he has chosen—his wife, who seems intent on making headlines as though they were some sort of royalty-obsessed Kardashians, and a media machine that churns out sympathy pieces like a factory line of self-serving narratives. In the days of yore, such behaviour would have led to a one-way ticket to the Tower, where the only entertainment would be the occasional visit from the executioner, brandishing his axe with the same disdain the British public now holds for the Sussexes.

And who could blame us? Harry’s relentless parade of grievances—his childhood traumas, his estranged family, his perpetual victimhood—has grown tiresome. It feels as if he has taken the lessons of his late mother, Princess Diana, and turned them into a sordid reality show, where every episode is marked by betrayal and an insatiable need for public approval. One might argue that Diana, had she been around, would have given him a stern talking-to, perhaps even a ‘get a grip, Harry’ lecture over a cup of tea.

As he and Meghan traipse around the globe, preaching the virtues of mental health while simultaneously making a mockery of their own familial ties, one can’t help but wonder if their antics might prompt a royal edict—‘Let them eat cake’ as they sit in their ivory tower, oblivious to the discontent brewing below. For in this land of pomp and pageantry, where tradition is revered, their antics are as out of place as a jester in a cathedral.

Ultimately, Harry won’t find himself in the Tower, but perhaps it’s time to ponder the legacy he is crafting for himself—one of disgrace rather than distinction. In a world that once revered him, he now stands as a cautionary tale, a prince turned pauper of public opinion. It’s a royal disgrace that would make any self-respecting Prince shudder in their boots. If only he could hear the whispers of history echoing through the stone walls, reminding him that treachery, once committed, has a way of finding its just desserts.

Meghan Markle: Unveiling the Dark Triad Persona

In the realm of celebrity, few figures have divided public opinion quite like Meghan Markle. From her fairy-tale wedding into the British royal family to her subsequent departure and public revelations, Meghan has captivated global attention with a charisma that masks deeper complexities.

Psychologists often refer to the Dark Triad personality traits—narcissism, Machiavellianism, and psychopathy—as a trifecta of malevolent characteristics. Meghan Markle, through her public persona and actions, appears to embody these traits in a way that has sparked controversy and intrigue.

• Narcissism: At the core of Meghan's persona lies an unyielding self-focus and a grandiose sense of self-importance. Her journey from actress to Duchess was marked by a calculated ascent, leveraging connections and opportunities to elevate her status. The decision to step back from royal duties was framed as a quest for personal authenticity, yet critics argue it was a narcissistic act of self-preservation, disregarding centuries-old traditions and protocols for her own aspirations.

• Machiavellianism: Meghan has demonstrated a shrewd ability to navigate the intricate webs of power and influence. From her strategic media appearances to her adept handling of public relations, she has portrayed herself as a victim while subtly manipulating public opinion to her advantage. Her alliances with influential figures and calculated interviews are seen as Machiavellian maneuvers aimed at securing sympathy and support, often at the expense of others' reputations.

• Psychopathy: Beneath her polished exterior lies a cool detachment and a lack of empathy characteristic of psychopathy. Critics point to her alleged mistreatment of staff and strained relationships within the royal family as evidence of callous disregard for others' feelings. Her ability to shift narratives effortlessly, from victim to activist, without genuine remorse or accountability, underscores a chilling disregard for the emotional impact of her actions on others.

The saga of Meghan Markle serves as a cautionary tale of the Dark Triad personality at play in the public eye. Her rise and subsequent controversies illustrate the seductive allure of power and the pitfalls of unchecked ambition. As she continues to navigate her post-royal life, observers are left to ponder the lasting impact of a woman whose path to fame was paved with ambition, controversy, and a profound impact on the institution she once sought to conquer.

In the realm of celebrity psychology, Meghan Markle stands as a compelling case study—a figure whose enigmatic charm and calculated maneuvers continue to fascinate and divide public opinion. Her journey serves as a stark reminder of the complexities of human nature and the enduring allure of the Dark Triad persona in the modern age.

author: @mommapanda5736
text:
Prince William’s Alleged Punch Would Have Settled Royal Feud Better Than Harry’s Whine Tour

Professional complainer and former British royal Harry Markle has done himself few favors in the leaked tidbits from his  memoir, from unflattering stories about his frostbitten manhood to his wife Meghan making comments about sister-in-law Kate’s pregnancy hormones (and then claiming to be the one who was “offended”).

In one of his many gripes, the defrocked prince complains about an argument with his older brother William in 2019 after William confronted Harry over Meghan’s “difficult,” “rude,” and “abrasive” behavior. After the spat escalated, Harry writes that William:


    …called me another name, then came at me. It all happened so fast. So very fast. He grabbed me by the collar, ripping my necklace, and he knocked me to the floor. I landed on the dog’s bowl, which cracked under my back, the pieces cutting into me. I lay there for a moment, dazed, then got to my feet and told him to get out.

The Guardian, which obtained the passage from the   book   SPARE    further reported:

    Harry writes that William urged him to hit back, citing fights they had as children. Harry says he refused to do so. William left, Harry says, then returned “looking regretful, and apologised”.

I assume Harry thought the inclusion of that allegation in his memoir reflected well on himself. But from the limited context of the excerpt, I can’t help wishing the brothers had come to blows there and then, potentially saving the rest of us from having to watch their family gripes play out publicly for years. William’s fisticuffs would have been a healthier, more effective means of settling the family drama than Harry’s strategy of cutting off his entire family and firing snide complaints at them from the pages of gossip magazines.

Of course, the best-case scenario for hashing out family feuds is usually a frank conversation. There will never be a better how-to guide for conflict resolution than that which Christ himself offered in Matthew 18. I’m not arguing that a well-placed punch is the ideal, Jesus-endorsed way to end an argument: It’s certainly not, although there are clear circumstances of biblically sanctioned blows.

But it is true that resolving issues directly, between offended and offender, and removing cause for a festering grudge is a healthier (and, relatedly, a more biblical) means of conflict resolution than waging a covert war behind each other’s backs. Most conflicts don’t require throwing punches. But none require going on daytime TV and book tours to trash family members while capitalizing on the fight with Spotify and Netflix deals.

Harry writes, the Guardian says, “that William urged him to hit back, citing fights they had as children.”

“Come on, hit me, you’ll feel better if you hit me,” William allegedly said. “Come on, we always used to fight.”

In a Sunday interview with ITV, Harry recalled the brothers used to “fight all the time” as children, from “shoot[ing] each other with BB guns” to having “firework fights.” (I guess that’s what you do when you’re a privileged prince and can’t just use your fists like the common folk?)

“I can pretty much guarantee today that if I wasn’t doing therapy sessions like I was and being able to process that anger and frustration, that I would’ve fought back, 100 percent,” Harry confessed in the interview. Maybe if he had fought back, the brothers’ dust-up could have been resolved then — and the rest of us might never have had to hear about it.

What Harry should have learned from those childhood tousles is how to get over a gripe, and how to pick battles wisely in the first place. Is the comment you’re butthurt about worth a sore jaw? If not, it’s also not worth burning family bridges by leaking your gripes to any magazine that will listen.

In the hands of wise parents, the fights kids get themselves into — verbal or physical — are an arena to teach kids how to handle conflict. You learn to forgive afterward, and eventually, to evaluate whether something is worth fighting about beforehand. You learn which forms of expressing your feelings are healthy and effective, and which ones aren’t. You also learn that there are worse things in the world than getting your rear end handed to you (such as: alienating yourself from your family). You learn communication and compromise. It’s a messy process, but it works a whole lot better than never speaking to each other again — something you can’t do when you’re a kid and you share a bathroom with the other combatant.

I’m certain, growing up in the thick of their parents’ explosive divorce, the bickering princes missed out on a healthy model of conflict resolution. Letting things come to blows is a sign that failed communication has happened already — but it also ensures that the resentments come to a head immediately, and usually results in some kind of patch-up afterward, rather than allowing those resentments to grow exponentially.

Unfortunately for the royals (and for the rest of us who have to watch them air each other’s dirty laundry), Harry didn’t settle his grievances with his brother via a private scuffle when they had the chance. Instead, he’s throwing punches through the inflammatory channels of podcasts, talk shows, and book deals, each of which shrinks the chances of real resolution.

At least a fistfight is more genuine. And probably more pleasant — I’d rather be on the receiving end of a shove than have to read Harry’s book.

Most conflicts don’t require throwing punches. None require going on daytime TV and book tours to trash family members.

   (   written by Elle Purnell is the elections editor at The Federalist. Her work has been featured by Fox Business, RealClearPolitics, the Tampa Bay Times, and the Independent Women's Forum. She received her B.A. in government from Patrick Henry College with a minor in journalism. Follow her on Twitter @_ellepurnell.)

Is it just me, or is there something utterly absurd about Harry and Meghan’s claim to integrity? Their high-profile chat with Oprah felt more like a prime-time soap opera than a royal disclosure, exposing family matters with all the decorum of a reality show. Trust? That’s long gone.

How can we take their complaints about media intrusion seriously when they’ve wielded the press like a weapon, crafting a narrative that’s equal parts victimhood and self-promotion? They’ve laid bare their lives in the most scandalous way imaginable, creating a spectacle out of what should have been private. It’s as if they’ve mistaken the royal family for a Netflix series, where ratings trump reality and the family business is mere entertainment.

Let’s talk about those awards, shall we? Harry’s got a Ripple of Hope Award and a shiny spot in the Living Legends of Aviation Hall of Fame. Royalty, traditionally the bestowers of honours, now seems to have entered a bizarre game of musical chairs where everyone gets a trophy for merely existing. The public’s reaction? Well, it’s as divided as ever. Some lap up their revelations, while others are left cringing at the sheer hypocrisy. Their willingness to exploit their royal status while claiming victimhood is a masterclass in contradiction.

And let’s not forget Harry’s military background—a legacy of service that now feels tarnished by his endless pursuit of fame. Instead of honouring that heritage, he seems hell-bent on dismantling it, trading dignity for headlines.

In the end, the combination of their media theatrics and the audacity of their royal status has cultivated a sense of betrayal that’s hard to shake off. If integrity were a currency, Harry and Meghan are already bankrupt.

In the latest chapter of the Sussexes’ post-palace saga, the power couple known for “escaping” the royal family’s golden cage seems to have run into a bit of a gilded problem of their own. Enter 𝘐𝘯𝘛𝘰𝘶𝘤𝘩’s newest headline: “𝘋𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘰𝘺𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘺 𝘎𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘥!”—not exactly the fairy-tale ending they had in mind when they departed Britain’s shores, proclamations of independence trailing behind them.

Let’s dissect this “$100 million empire collapse,” shall we? For two people who once bemoaned the scrutiny and pressures of being in the royal fishbowl, Harry and Meghan sure seemed to make a swift U-turn back into the spotlight, albeit a more lucrative one. Who knew privacy could be so profitable? Between lucrative Netflix deals, star-studded Spotify podcasts, and tell-all book advances, they proved that fame can indeed be sold by the pound—until, it appears, the empire built on grievances and carefully crafted victimhood narratives began showing some cracks.

“𝘈𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘉𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘴! screams the subhead, as if the world needed reminding of their extravagances. For Harry, the young prince who once dared to tell the world his father had financially abandoned him (while living in a multimillion-dollar Montecito mansion), financial reality may now be arriving with the grace of a stagecoach collision. As for Meghan, the transformation from a self-styled humanitarian to the Duchess of Dollar Signs has not exactly gone unnoticed.

And now, it seems, the “reckless royals” have reached the inevitable end of their fairy tale: not with the pomp and pageantry they once denounced, but with headlines about their “𝘈𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘴!” Yes, the allure of billionaire ambitions was just too tantalising to resist, even for those who claimed to be fleeing the trappings of aristocratic privilege. One might say their undoing wasn’t so much greed as a relentless pursuit of relevance—wrapped in the velvet of luxury and sprinkled with a hint of delusion.

So, as the Sussex empire teeters, perhaps this isn’t the fairy tale they envisioned when they traded Buckingham Palace for a Californian castle. Instead of newfound freedom, it seems they’ve simply exchanged one gilded cage for another—only this time, the bars are forged by ambition, avarice, and a ravenous pursuit of fame.

author: @kansasrose2909
text:
Does Meghan Markle Want Us To Hate Her?

There are plenty of reasons to hate Meghan Markle, so why did she just give us a whole Netflix season of more ammo? From stabbing the royal family in the back after having her entire life subsidized by British taxpayers to earning $25 million from Spotify for a few middling podcast episodes, Markle is a villainous figure who rakes in hate, not the praise and fandom she is clearly desperate for.

When Markle made her grand return to Instagram this New Year after dramatically quitting social media in 2021, it wasn’t for funsies. It was to announce and promote her new eight-part Netflix show, “With Love, Meghan.” 
From the teaser trailer she shared, the series appears to be Markle’s best attempt at LARPing Martha Stewart with her celebrity pals on her $15 million Montecito compound. “I’m going to share some tips and tricks,” Markle says as she peruses the flower market and sprinkles dried flowers on top of glazed donuts.

“We’re not in the pursuit of perfection. We’re in the pursuit of joy!” she exclaims with an acute degree of inauthenticity. The copy is dripping with feigned platitudes and the images are suspiciously rife with royal ripoffs. This trailer is so cringe-inducing that it physically makes my eyes twitch.

What’s most surprising about this product is that there was no one close enough to her to wave their hands and gently guide her in the complete opposite direction. When Netflix came knocking, what pitches did she turn down when she opted for this Ballerina Farm wannabe vanity project? Did no one who loves her suggest a series with a bit more sympathetic angle? A reality show where she helps down-and-out folks find a new home? A docu-series where she visits small, but beautiful American cities, highlighting everyday heroes?

The only plausible explanation for Markle’s vanity project is that she relishes victimhood so much that she doesn’t care what the haters say because their critiques and comments sustain her signature victim mentality. Knowing she will never be the beloved people’s princess like her late mother-in-law, she’s stopped trying and settled for the loathed queen of Montecito.

Let’s be honest—what was once a meaningful and respected initiative has turned into a shameless PR parade, thanks to the Man-Child Harry and his D-List Social Climber wife Meghan Markle. Instead of focusing on veterans, the Games have become Meghan’s designer-clad runway, complete with shallow photo ops that scream “Look at me!” more than “Support our heroes.” The mission of Invictus—celebrating resilience and unity—has been overshadowed by a vanity project designed to boost their tarnished reputations. The Invictus Games used to stand for something noble—a symbol of respect for those who served. Veterans deserve so much better than having their platform co-opted by a Man-Child and his Social Climber wife, who shamelessly exploit their sacrifices to stay relevant.  

It’s time for Invictus to return to its roots: empowering veterans—not boosting the egos of those who have tarnished its cause. Enough is enough.

author: @kansasrose2909
text:
Petty Woman: Meghan Markle Waves Goodbye To Her Rom-Com Dreams   THE END OF THE ROAD?

Not all fairy tales have happy endings, and for Princess Meghan the clock just chimed midnight and the spell has been broken. The coach is turning back into a pumpkin as we speak.

As a longtime Royal Family watcher, I admit to feeling shameless glee as I read the recent stories of Meghan and Harry striking out in Hollywood. It’s always fun to watch dire low-stakes predictions come true. Like many of you, I was appalled at the disrespect Meghan showed to her in-laws. Instead of respecting the Queen, Meghan, incredibly, seemed to be trying to compete with the Queen. She thought she was playing a game of “Survivor,” but she was the only one on the island who didn’t know how to make a fire.
A Long Way Down for the Duchess

For those not keeping track, Meghan and her nitwit ginger sidekick have been dropped by Spotify, reportedly losing half of the $50 million promised. She got $25 million for a measly 12 hours of a middling podcast featuring the richest and most famous women in the world complaining about how hard their lives are. Netflix is reportedly about to cut their $100 million deal short. They finished milking them dry of low-hanging tabloid family gossip, and just found out they have no Act 2.

Nothing is working out the way she dreamed it would. Meghan’s imagined billionaire lifestyle is turning into a mirage. Why? Because for some hilarious reason, the creative bigwigs in Hollywood believed Meghan when she promised that her and Harry would be able to provide oodles of monetizable entertainment content.  

I mean, yes, I am quite entertained by the spectacle, but schadenfreude is tough to monetize.
Meghan In Her Flop Era

Meghan’s predicament tells you everything about the people who run Hollywood. Imagine thinking that these two “f*cking grifters,” in the words of the Spotify exec who had to say no to Harry’s harebrained podcast ideas, would be a rich source of high-quality entertainment! 

I can’t help wondering how a D-list golddigger convinced these studio heads that her and the ginger mouth breather would somehow provide $150 million worth of streaming content. It turns out that they’re only good at providing piles of steaming content, if you know what I mean.

I suppose it’s true, as movie producer Jackie Trehorn tells the Dude in “The Big Lebowski,” standards have fallen in entertainment. Since the Sussexes first ditched their careers as legit royalty and started groping for ephemeral Hollywood royalty, my fellow Meghan hobbyists and I have enjoyed a goldmine of unintentional comedy. She’s the Benny Hill of pampered Montecito trophy wives, always running downhill chased by imaginary paparazzi. 

She’s been a source of delight since the early days when she was using a Sharpie to write inspirational messages on bananas to street prostitutes in England. “You are brave.” “You are loved.” Then the cringe-worthy trek through the thousand micro-aggressions she endured at the hands of her sister-in-law Catherine. Did she not realize everyone saw it for what it was: pure jealousy?

But now we come to the era of Meghan Markle, entertainment content creator. The latest chapter in the Meghan character arc is about the content she and hapless Harry are trying to pitch to their paymasters in Beverly Hills. It was clear that her long slide back into C-list obscurity had begun when I read an incredible tidbit in the trades earlier this year. Meghan was talking about her new content ideas she was working on for her “media production company.” See, it’s already funny! 

Meghan gushed to a Variety reporter: “For scripted, we want to think about how we can evolve from that same space and do something fun! It doesn’t always have to be so serious. Like a good rom-com. Don’t we miss them? I miss them so much. I’ve probably watched ‘When Harry Met Sally’ a million times. And all the Julia Roberts rom-coms. We need to see those again.”

We do? Rom-coms? I mean, yeah, it would be wonderful to have good movies again, of any genre. But with Meghan in charge, imagine the scripts she would commission. “When Harry Met Meghan, the Oppressed and Suicidal Actress.” “How to Lose a Prince in 10 Days.”  “10 Things I Hate About Kate.” “The Meghan Markle Story, Starring Meghan Markle.” 

That last one’s more of a tragicomedy than a rom-com, sorry. But I understand why she wants to make Julia Roberts-style romantic comedies. After all, just a few years ago, she was lurking on Hollywood Boulevard auditioning for her big break when a prince in an Aston Martin cruised by and whisked her away to his palace. She has lived a real-life Cinderella story. Only this one may not have quite the same ending.

As Jeremy Zimmer, the CEO of United Talent Agency, one of the largest Hollywood talent agencies dished during Cannes to every reporter within earshot: “It turns out that Meghan Markle wasn’t a great audio talent, or necessarily has some kind of talent. And you know, just because you’re famous doesn’t mean you’re good at something.” 

Ouch. I wonder if Jeremy Zimmer has seen the latest desperate pitch Meghan made to Netflix; a girlboss rom-com called “Bad Manners” starring … Miss Havisham. The show is “a prequel to Charles Dickens’s 1861 novel Great Expectations which will focus on the character Miss Havisham… [the show] aims to shine a feminist light on the spinster, showing her as a ‘strong woman living in a patriarchal society.’”

Who says comedy is dead? Sign me up for this one!

The article ends with the ominous “it is unclear whether the show will get a green light from Netflix.” 

Meghan is learning, finally, the hardest lesson of all: real royalty may be hereditary, but Hollywood royalty has to be earned. Popularity matters. Likeability, in the end, is the only currency that matters if you wear no crown.

text:
Meghan Markle Is No People’s Princess Like Diana
In Prince Harry and Meghan Markle’s highly rated Oprah interview   the couple bitterly accused the British royal family of repulsive racism and avid jealousy. The couple slandered everyone, from accusing the royals of making comments about the skin tone of their son Archie, to claiming Duchess Kate made Markle cry before her wedding.

Throughout the interview, Harry made comparisons between his wife Meghan and his mother, the late Princess Diana, widely known as “the people’s princess.” Harry told Oprah things “really changed” for the couple after their 2018 Australia tour. “It was the first time that the family got to see how incredible [Meghan] is at the job,” Harry said.

Oprah then referenced scenes from the hit Netflix series “The Crown” during Prince Charles and Princess Diana’s tour through Australia in 1988. Prince Charles is seen becoming increasingly jealous of his glamorous and beloved wife who is fawned over by the people and the media.

Oprah asked Harry whether their tour of Australia “brought back memories” of his parents’ trip, saying: “Your father and your mother went there, and your mother was bedazzling. So, are you saying there were hints of jealousy [from the rest of the royal family]?”

“I just wish that we would all learn from the past,” Harry told Oprah, insinuating his family was in fact jealous of Meghan. “To see how effortless it was for Meghan to come into the family so quickly in Australia and across New Zealand, Fiji and Tonga, and just be able to connect with people…”

Of course, the media ate this up, and it’s obvious to those who follow royal family news closely that these were calculated and premeditated comments from Harry that have done exactly what he wanted — entice major media outlets like Vogue,Insider and USA Today to run clip bait-y headlines comparing Meghan to the legendary princess.

There’s just one problem. Diana was loved by the people. Meghan is only loved by leftist elites in Hollywood and the corporate media.
A Royal Copy-Cat

Meghan has been accused of desperately trying to emulate Diana, presumably in hopes of garnering sympathy and popularity from those who still love and miss the late princess.

Even though Diana is known for masterfully navigating the press to her advantage, in the end, the media became the source of her tragic demise. It isn’t hard to imagine that in Meghan’s pursuit to be the next Diana, she would try to paint herself as a second victim of the media.

However, Meghan’s victim narrative is ultimately unconvincing since the media initially doted on her. Even now, after all her reproachable behavior, the leftist corporate media is not only defending her and flattering her, but also shaming anyone, notably Piers Morgan, who doesn’t do the same.

Meghan’s sit-down interview with Oprah had eerie similarities to Diana’s Panorama tell-all, where Diana confided, “there were three of us in this marriage,” in reference to her husband Charles’s affair with Camilla Parker Bowles. For her interview, Meghan wore a black dress with a plunging v-neck, just like Diana.

𝐈𝐬 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐨𝐱𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐞𝐠𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐥𝐞? 

That’s the question on everyone’s lips as the Duke of Sussex slowly, and somewhat tragically, comes to grips with the storm he’s waded into. For years, the world watched with morbid curiosity as Prince Harry fell under the spell of the cable actress who seemed to promise him the kind of liberation he thought he craved. But now, it appears the fog might be lifting.

Ever since he and Meghan Markle packed up their royal obligations and moved stateside, Harry has been like a lost puppy. Yes, he’s had the bright lights of Montecito and the comforting hum of Netflix millions to keep him warm, but let’s not pretend that anything about their lives has been a fairy tale. He’s gone from being one of the most loved members of the royal family to a footnote on the latest podcast ranking. Once a cheeky, beloved prince, he now seems diminished, frequently wielding accusations against his own flesh and blood, all in the name of “truth-telling” while sporting a perpetual look of someone who's swallowed a bee.

Of course, Meghan clings to the spotlight with the fervour of someone whose star is slowly dimming. The glossy sheen she’s worked so hard to maintain is starting to crack. But as the carefully curated image begins to crumble, people are starting to ask: Has Harry been played? The relentless pursuit of victimhood, the never-ending stream of grievances, the lawsuits, the interviews where they professed they just wanted privacy while eagerly airing their private lives—it’s all starting to look a bit tiresome, isn’t it? It’s as if Meghan brings chaos and strife wherever she goes, leaving a trail of scorched earth behind her. And now, Harry, standing alone in the ashes, might be waking up to the realisation that he’s not a leading man in a romcom. He’s the fall guy in a badly scripted melodrama.

The cracks in their fortress of solidarity are hard to ignore. From awkward public appearances where Harry looks increasingly weary, to reports of them living “separate lives,” it’s clear that the Duke of Sussex’s fairytale with the duchess might not have the happy ending he envisioned. Could it be that Harry is slowly but surely realising the poison in the air? That aligning himself so completely with Meghan’s seemingly endless vendettas has isolated him from everyone who once cared for him? The court of public opinion has shifted, and not in their favour.

Perhaps Harry is beginning to understand that the woman he thought was his greatest ally may, in fact, be his Achilles heel. Meghan’s love for the spotlight is insatiable, and Harry’s been dragged along for the ride, his own identity slowly eroded. Meanwhile, she flourishes as the victim-turned-heroine in her own fantasy, playing to the gallery of sycophants while carefully casting Harry in the role of the sacrificial lamb.

As he surveys the debris of the bridges burned and relationships fractured, one can only wonder—how much longer before Harry tires of this reality show existence? The toxicity surrounding Meghan Markle has become undeniable, but the question now is: does Harry finally see it?

It’s hard to imagine a more spectacular fall from grace. Meghan Markle, a former cable TV actress, married into the British Royal Family and found herself with a title, a global platform, and all the trappings of royalty. But this wasn’t Tinseltown—there were protocols, centuries of tradition, and an expectation to serve the British people. And here’s where the Sussexes’ story shifts from fairy tale to farce.

Let's be clear: when they first announced they were stepping back, many Brits wished them luck on their new life. Their decision to seek more privacy and independence didn’t raise many eyebrows initially. But it was their behaviour afterwards that truly soured public opinion.

What they did next is the stuff of modern hubris. First came the 𝘖𝘱𝘳𝘢𝘩 𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘪𝘦𝘸, a two-hour primetime spectacular where grievances were aired in the most public way possible. Meghan, who played the “𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘴𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘳” card at every turn, presented herself as a victim of a royal machine that allegedly ignored her mental health struggles. For Harry, it was a platform to lay bare years of family resentment, tarnishing the reputations of the very people who once adored him. Royalty, by its nature, thrives on discretion, loyalty, and service, but the Sussexes were out for blood—𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘪𝘳 narrative was all that mattered.

The whining didn’t stop there. Harry’s memoir 𝘚𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘦 only deepened the chasm, dragging up petty sibling squabbles with Prince William, tantrums over tiaras, and accusations that reeked of entitlement and narcissism. Once the couple cried racism and abandonment, any residual goodwill began evaporating at lightning speed.

Their behaviour screamed hypocrisy. How could they demand privacy while signing a multimillion-dollar Netflix deal to expose the very family they abandoned? Their repeated claims of victimhood wore thin—when you trade castles for Montecito mansions, it’s hard to sell yourself as oppressed. No one cared about them leaving the royal family, but they certainly cared about the Sussexes playing both sides: royal victims and Tinseltown celebrities, crying injustice while cashing in.

What’s even more damning is their irrelevance. The world has moved on. Meghan’s Spotify podcast flopped, their Netflix ventures struggled, and their post-royal projects seem like nothing more than vanity projects. Meanwhile, King Charles, William, and Catherine continue to quietly go about the business of serving the public—a stark contrast to Harry and Meghan’s continuous soap opera.

The Sussexes were handed it all, only to throw it away in a grand gesture of self-sabotage. From royal glitz to grasping at fame, their story has shifted from one of potential to one of pathos. No one forced them out, but their behaviour post-exit ensured they are never welcomed back.

Meghan Markle has turned her need for control into a public spectacle, constantly reminding both Harry—and the world—who’s really in charge. The so-called 'independent feminist' has manipulated and emasculated her husband to the point where he’s convinced he needs her, not the other way around. Every public appearance becomes a desperate display of clinging and clutching, as she makes sure no one forgets who’s pulling the strings in their ‘power couple’ dynamic. 

Her inability to keep her hands to herself, especially in professional settings, shatters her claims of being independent. Instead, it highlights just how dependent she is on Harry’s status. Meghan knows her place in the spotlight is fragile at best, and she overcompensates by diminishing Harry’s shine, even at events meant to honor him. This isn’t just insecurity on display; it’s a calculated effort to keep him under her control, ensuring he never thinks for himself or steals the spotlight. 

Her opportunistic tendencies have earned her quite the reputation. Meghan clings onto anyone she can use to her advantage, and this has become well-known in Hollywood circles. It’s one of the many reasons no one’s calling her for collaborations, scripts, or deals. Designers avoid her, and she’s seen as difficult, selfish, and entitled, all while believing she’s far more important than she really is—just because she managed to convince a clueless prince to marry her.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲: 𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐁𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐍𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐯𝐞

Prince Harry, once the shining light of the royal family, has now become a figure of contempt in Britain, a man who has not only turned his back on his family but, more egregiously, sold out his country. His actions over the past few years have burned every last bridge, leaving the British public with nothing but scorn for the man who once stood shoulder to shoulder with the people.

The Oprah interview was the tipping point. It was here that Harry, complicit in silence, allowed Meghan Markle to imply that a member of the royal family had concerns about the skin colour of their son, Archie. The accusation was seismic, sending shockwaves through the UK. But what made this worse—what made it utterly unforgivable—was Harry’s inaction. His failure to stand up for his family while his ailing grandfather, Prince Philip, was in his final days showed a callous disregard for the pain it would cause. No matter the issues he may have had behind closed doors, to go on international television and sully the name of the institution that raised him was seen by many as nothing short of treachery.

And as if the Oprah debacle wasn’t bad enough, we were later subjected to 𝘏𝘢𝘳𝘳𝘺 & 𝘔𝘦𝘨𝘩𝘢𝘯, the Netflix mockumentary thinly veiled as a love letter to themselves but in truth, a very public airing of grievances. It was here that Meghan’s mocking of the royal tradition of curtsying to Queen Elizabeth shocked us Brits. With a poorly executed theatrical bow and a laughable comparison to medieval times, she belittled a gesture that symbolises respect and duty—values the British monarchy stands for. And Harry? He smirked. His silence, again, was deafening. How could any grandson, raised in the folds of such tradition, allow his wife to mock the woman who represented so much to so many?

The British people watched, aghast. That smirk—that quiet complicity—was a betrayal not just of his family, but of us, the British public who had once held him in such high regard. Queen Elizabeth, beloved and respected, was the embodiment of duty and grace, and for Harry to stand idly by as she was mocked before her passing will never be forgiven. The wound is deep, and it’s raw.

Then came the memoir 𝘚𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘦. If the Netflix series was a veiled attack, 𝘚𝘱𝘢𝘳𝘦 was an all-out assault. Page after page of grievances, personal attacks on his father and brother, intimate family moments laid bare for the world to see. The British public has always respected the monarchy’s ability to keep private matters within the palace walls. Harry tore that tradition apart. And for what? A quick buck, a bit of global attention. The title of ‘spare’ may have haunted him his whole life, but now it’s clear: the role he once resented is one he’s embraced—no longer a prince, but a spare to the very values that once defined him.

For us Brits, it isn’t just the content of his attacks that hurts—it’s the fact that he’s chosen to air them so publicly, so vindictively. The monarchy is not just his family; it is the backbone of British history, culture, and identity. To see it so easily discarded and vilified by one of its own is a wound that may never heal.

No, Britain will not forgive Harry. The man who was once the cheeky prince with a ready smile and a heart for service has become a symbol of betrayal. He has betrayed his family, his country, and his role in history. And for that, there is no going back.

And Meghan we can never forgive your behavior either.

As for Meghan, the duchess who would modernise the monarchy, she quickly became better known for her rotating staff roster and pre-dawn emails than for any philanthropic deeds. Dubbed ‘Duchess Difficult’, she managed to clear out the palace quicker than Brexit negotiations. You have to hand it to her, though—who else could take a royal and transform him into a Hollywood house-husband doing mental health talks and fidgeting in interviews?

After all, it takes a certain kind of magic to convince a prince to turn his back on a literal kingdom in exchange for a deal with Spotify, only to have it go bust. And who could forget their $100 million Netflix ‘special’, where they spent hours recounting how tough life was inside royal palaces that most people would give their left arm to live in. Harry, once an army officer and people’s prince, now finds himself as a glorified extra in Meghan’s ongoing production of “Meghan’s World.”

The turning point must have been the New York ‘car chase’ debacle. What was sold as a high-octane thriller involving paparazzi turned out to be an awkward taxi ride that made the royals seem more out of touch than ever. At that point, it became clear that the fairy tale was wearing thin. No crowns, no tiaras—just two people bemoaning their lot in life from behind the gates of their $14 million mansion.

And now, with rumours swirling that their marriage is on the rocks, it’s hard not to wonder if Harry is finally seeing what the rest of us have known for a while. He thought he was getting his happily-ever-after. Instead, he’s found himself as the frog in a very one-sided fairy tale, waiting for a kiss that will never come.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐨𝐲𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐦: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐀𝐀𝐀𝐆𝐇 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐄𝐜𝐡𝐨𝐞𝐝 𝐀𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐥𝐝

In the grand theatre of royal melodrama, it appears that Harry and Meghan have firmly established themselves as the chief protagonists of the blame game. Like clockwork, their monotonous dirge of complaints plays on a never-ending loop, each note dripping with self-pity and delusion. The attached cartoon, with its scathing "Mr & Mrs WAAAGH," perfectly encapsulates the emotional petulance that has come to define their public personas. 

It’s always 𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘳𝘺𝘣𝘰𝘥𝘺 𝘦𝘭𝘴𝘦'𝘴 𝘧𝘢𝘶𝘭𝘵 for the Sussexes, as they thrash and kick their way through each grievance, unable—or unwilling—to accept any responsibility for their own missteps. Perhaps it's the cold shoulder from their family, or the world’s failure to recognise the sheer brilliance of their global "mission." Or maybe it's just that those pesky royal protocols dared to exist, cramping their Hollywood aspirations. One minute they preach compassion from their Montecito mansion, and the next, they’re busy launching volleys of blame, alleging betrayal by family members they once claimed to love.

Let’s call it what it is: an ongoing temper tantrum of epic proportions, masked as noble defiance. Poor Harry, still stuck in a psychological headlock of “mummy issues” and a never-ending spiral of resentment. And Meghan, with her quivering lip and tearful declarations of being “𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘮𝘰𝘴𝘵 𝘣𝘶𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘦𝘥 𝘱𝘦𝘳𝘴𝘰𝘯 𝘪𝘯 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘭𝘥,” trots out every cliché in the victim playbook. Yet for a couple who loathe the monarchy, they seem perfectly happy to clutch onto their royal titles—when it suits them, of course.

The genius of this cartoon lies not just in its hilarious caricature of the couple flailing on the ground like children denied their latest toy, but in its profound truth. “Mr & Mrs WAAAGH!” indeed—forever wailing into the void about the injustices heaped upon them, with no self-awareness that their self-inflicted PR carnage has burned every bridge they once held dear.

For Harry, who once epitomised a cheeky, lovable royal, his descent into this abyss of public whining is nothing short of tragic. Gone are the days of the sturdy, stoic prince, replaced by a man seemingly addicted to grievance. And Meghan, well, Hollywood didn’t care before she found a prince, and the Palace seems to care even less now. The fairy tale is over, and in its place, we are left with the endless 𝘞𝘈𝘈𝘈𝘎𝘏 of a couple who simply cannot stop blaming the world for their downfall.

What the Sussexes fail to understand—perhaps because they are too busy casting stones—is that their attempts to shift the narrative only reinforce their image as spoiled, self-indulgent, and utterly tone-deaf. They sit atop their multimillion-dollar empire, professing victimhood, while the world looks on, exhausted by the unrelenting cries of "woe is me."

In the end, the cartoon's portrayal is spot on. There they are, Harry and Meghan, forever locked in a cycle of kicking and screaming, oblivious to the fact that the only people responsible for their misery are the ones staring back at them in the mirror.

Consider the tale of her supposed close pals. There’s the loyal 𝘑𝘦𝘴𝘴𝘪𝘤𝘢 𝘔𝘶𝘭𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘦𝘺, who was once the poster child for Meghan’s inner circle. Then there’s her frosty relationship with former castmates from 𝘚𝘶𝘪𝘵𝘴. Once a valued part of their ensemble, Meghan has exhibited all the warmth of a polar vortex since her ascent into royal life. When she didn’t receive the glowing endorsement she craved, she retreated into the shadows, leaving her former friends clutching their pearls in disbelief. 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐮𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐱 𝐄𝐦𝐩𝐢𝐫𝐞: 𝐁𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐭 𝐨𝐧 𝐆𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞, 𝐓𝐨𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐝

In the latest chapter of the Sussexes’ post-palace saga, the power couple known for “escaping” the royal family’s golden cage seems to have run into a bit of a gilded problem of their own. Enter 𝘐𝘯𝘛𝘰𝘶𝘤𝘩’s newest headline: “𝘋𝘦𝘴𝘵𝘳𝘰𝘺𝘦𝘥 𝘣𝘺 𝘎𝘳𝘦𝘦𝘥!”—not exactly the fairy-tale ending they had in mind when they departed Britain’s shores, proclamations of independence trailing behind them.

Let’s dissect this “$100 million empire collapse,” shall we? For two people who once bemoaned the scrutiny and pressures of being in the royal fishbowl, Harry and Meghan sure seemed to make a swift U-turn back into the spotlight, albeit a more lucrative one. Who knew privacy could be so profitable? Between lucrative Netflix deals, star-studded Spotify podcasts, and tell-all book advances, they proved that fame can indeed be sold by the pound—until, it appears, the empire built on grievances and carefully crafted victimhood narratives began showing some cracks.

“𝘈𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘉𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘴! screams the subhead, as if the world needed reminding of their extravagances. For Harry, the young prince who once dared to tell the world his father had financially abandoned him (while living in a multimillion-dollar Montecito mansion), financial reality may now be arriving with the grace of a stagecoach collision. As for Meghan, the transformation from a self-styled humanitarian to the Duchess of Dollar Signs has not exactly gone unnoticed.

And now, it seems, the “reckless royals” have reached the inevitable end of their fairy tale: not with the pomp and pageantry they once denounced, but with headlines about their “𝘈𝘤𝘵𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘭𝘪𝘬𝘦 𝘣𝘪𝘭𝘭𝘪𝘰𝘯𝘢𝘪𝘳𝘦𝘴!” Yes, the allure of billionaire ambitions was just too tantalising to resist, even for those who claimed to be fleeing the trappings of aristocratic privilege. One might say their undoing wasn’t so much greed as a relentless pursuit of relevance—wrapped in the velvet of luxury and sprinkled with a hint of delusion.

So, as the Sussex empire teeters, perhaps this isn’t the fairy tale they envisioned when they traded Buckingham Palace for a Californian castle. Instead of newfound freedom, it seems they’ve simply exchanged one gilded cage for another—only this time, the bars are forged by ambition, avarice, and a ravenous pursuit of fame.

author: @mommapanda5736
text:
𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐥𝐞𝐬 

Allow me a moment of reflection—a moment to thank South Park for saying, in blunt cartoon form, what we’ve all been thinking for far too long. It took a pair of animated misfits to finally unmask the Sussexes as the preening, privacy-loving paradoxes they are. And there they were: Harry, the wide-eyed prince who traded a crown for celebrity handshakes, and Meghan, the self-styled activist whose causes seem to end where the camera cuts. In one fell swoop, 𝘚𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘩 𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘬 delivered what the world had been silently begging for: a full-throttle takedown of the Southparkles and their spectacular descent into self-parody.  

Remember when these two high-tailed it out of Britain, bemoaning the shackles of royal life, only to shove their brand into every screen from Montecito to Manhattan? The escape to “freedom” quickly turned into a relentless self-promotional tour, complete with a glossy Netflix deal, weepy docu-series, and a Spotify podcast that droned on as vapidly as the platitudes they preach. Privacy, it turns out, is a state of mind—for the Sussexes, it’s one they scream about from every headline, podcast, and interview, their own echo chamber of self-pity.

𝘚𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘩 𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘬 didn’t invent this farce; it merely held up a merciless mirror. They nailed Harry’s unearned martyrdom and Meghan’s shapeshifting causes, two perfectly polished caricatures of victimhood turned luxury brand. And what do the ‘Southparkles’ do in response? More finger-pointing, more grievances, another episode of “How the Palace Wronged Us,” as if the world hadn’t long ago tuned out. The Queen managed seventy years of scrutiny with grace, but two years of negative press have Harry and Meghan running to their lawyers—confirming that, yes, the only thing they’re actually good at is complaining.

In truth, 𝘚𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘩 𝘗𝘢𝘳𝘬 gave them a rare gift: the one thing that’s been missing in the echo chamber of their own making—perspective. But, of course, Harry and Meghan can’t see the humour. The irony is so thick you could spread it on toast: two people who desperately crave the spotlight, now reduced to cartoon characters in the cultural joke they can’t escape. Perhaps they should finally do us all a favour and give us the one thing they promised but never delivered—a quiet exit. Then again, where would the profit be in that?

Southpark,  what could you make of this pair's recent  DISASTER TOURISM ??   we await your rendition eagerly.

author: @mommapanda5736
text:
𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐢𝐧 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐞𝐨𝐩𝐥𝐞’𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬: 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐫𝐲’𝐬 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐥 𝐨𝐟 𝐇𝐲𝐩𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐲
Harry encourages Meghan to Cash in      or does he?

Oh, the irony. Here we have the Duke and Duchess of Sussex—those self-styled champions of “privacy” who fled the royal fold to pursue their “authentic” lives—caught in the act of their true pursuit: piles upon piles of cash. Prince Harry, grinning like a Cheshire cat, cracks a whip with all the enthusiasm of a ringmaster orchestrating his own spectacle, while Meghan clutches a bulging sack of money, her grin an unmistakable sign of how far she’s come from cable TV to the centre of a money-making circus.   What about those two bags of product she is seen
clutching in the fire zone area.   What is in those two bags?

And lying beneath this grand parade, the ghostly presence of Princess Diana—“The People’s Princess”—whose memory Harry has used to justify his treachery. The very mother he claims to honour, positioned here as a quiet, helpless spectator in the spectacle he’s made of her legacy. Diana, who genuinely connected with people and dedicated herself to causes that meant something, now finds her image entangled in the cash-fuelled carnival Harry and Meghan have orchestrated in her name.

With banknotes and gold coins cascading like confetti, you can practically hear the ka-ching echoing through Montecito. From Netflix docuseries to tell-all memoirs, the Sussex duo has turned “public service” into “personal profit.” Privacy? They only wanted privacy from the obligations, it seems—not from the cash and cameras that come with the royal titles they claim to despise.

If Diana were here, she’d give her son a royal dressing-down for exploiting her memory to line his own pockets. Because for all Harry’s posturing, he’s not walking in his mother’s footsteps; he’s trampling on her memory.  Sad.
